The input table is an excerpted **table of contents** for the SOFiSTiK manual “**BEMESS – Design of Plates and Shells**” (BEMESS Manual, Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146). It is organized hierarchically with **section numbering**, **section titles**, and **page references** (e.g., “2-1”, “2-2”, etc.), indicating where each topic begins in the manual. The table also includes surrounding contextual text describing program capabilities (design according to codes, extraction of extreme stresses, serviceability checks, and punching checks), but the actual structured table entries are the contents lines shown in the screenshot.

## Table structure
- **Rows**: Each row corresponds to a **topic** or **subtopic**.
- **Columns**: The table is effectively represented as three components per entry:
  1. **Section/Chapter number** (e.g., “2.1”, “2.2.3”)
  2. **Title** (e.g., “Bending Design of Reinforced Concrete”)
  3. **Page pointer** (e.g., “2-1”, “2-2”, etc.)
- **Hierarchy**: Increasing decimal depth denotes more specific subsections:
  - Top-level: “2.1 … 2.5 …”
  - Subsections: “2.2.1 … 2.2.11 …”
  - Deeper still: e.g., “2.5.8 … 2.5.11 …”

## Content coverage (what the sections are about)
The excerpt focuses on **theoretical principles** and then expands into key design/check categories:

1. **Chapter 2: Theoretical Principles** (implied by heading)
2. **Bending design of reinforced concrete** (section “2.2”) with many detailed sub-processes:
   - General comments and reinforcement meshes
   - Concrete compression stress and compression reinforcement
   - Minimum reinforcement for pressed cross sections
   - Tendons
   - Design procedures according to **Baumann (CTRL LAY 0)**, **layer design (CTRL LAY 1)**, and **sandwich design per Eurocode prEN Annex G (CTRL LAY 2)**
   - **Steel fiber concrete** and “other design codes”
3. **Service load checks** (section “2.3”)
   - Minimum/required topics including crack width control (without/with direct calculation)
   - SLS stress range and fatigue considerations
4. **Shear checks** (section “2.4”)
   - With “Other Design Codes” subitem
5. **Punching checks** (section “2.5”)
   - General information
   - Column input and control parameters
   - Handling different column situations: inner, edge, corner columns
   - Shear and bending design at the column
   - Wall end/corner special features
   - Punching at foundations and consistency of the procedure at checks
   - Punching check in multi-dimensional systems
   - V-Ed analysis out of MAXIMA superposition loadcases
   - Other design codes
6. Later entries indicate further topics:
   - **Linear stress determination** (section “6”)
   - **Disk structures** (section “7”)
   - **Volume elements** (section “8”)

## Notes for RAG usage
- The “page” values are **not full page numbers**, but manual-style references (e.g., “2-14”), useful for locating topics within the document.
- This table is best indexed as a **navigation/semantic map** to find where specific theoretical components (bending, serviceability/cracks, shear, punching) are described in the manual.

The provided table is an excerpt from the “Input Description” section of the SOFiSTiK **BEMESS – Design of Plates and Shells** manual (BEMESS Manual, Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146). It functions as a **table of contents / index** that enumerates the major **input blocks** available in the BEMESS program, along with the corresponding **section identifiers** and **page references**.

### Structure and content
The table lists entries from **3.1 through 3.25**, each representing a specific category of input or control data. Each row follows the pattern:

- **Label**: either a full description (e.g., “Input Language”) or an abbreviation (e.g., “NORМ – Default Design Code”).
- **Brief meaning**: what the input block controls/defines.
- **Page number**: where detailed documentation for that block begins (e.g., “3-3”, “3-26”).
- Some abbreviation lines also contain **sub-entries** (noted in this excerpt for “CTRL” and “CORE”).

### Rows (inputs) and their described purpose
- **3.1 Input Language** — introduces the language/format for entering BEMESS inputs.
- **3.2 Input Records** — describes the structure of records used for input data.
- **3.3 NORM – Default Design Code** — selects the default design code used for subsequent calculations.
- **3.4 CTRL – Control of the Design** — general design control parameters; includes **3.4.1 CORE – Parallel computation control**.
- **3.5 REIN – Title of the design case** — naming/identification of a design case related to reinforcement.
- **3.6 CRAC – Control of the Service Load Checks** — parameters controlling checks related to serviceability.
- **3.7 MRF – Minimum Reinforcement Checks** — defines settings for minimum reinforcement requirements.
- **3.8 SHFT – Offset Value for Shift Rule** — configuration for applying an offset in the “shift rule” (likely for redistribution/positioning logic in reinforcement design).
- **3.9 NSTR – SLS Checks** — settings for **SLS (serviceability limit state)** checks.
- **3.10 MAT – Input of Material Properties** — defines material property parameters used by the design.
- **3.11 GEOM – Input of the Cross Section** — geometry of the structural element/cross-section input.
- **3.12 DIRE – Definition of Orthogonal Two-course Reinforcement** — reinforcement definition for orthogonal two-layer/two-course layouts.
- **3.13 THRE – Definition of Skew 2- and 3-course Reinforcement** — reinforcement definition for skewed 2- and 3-course systems.
- **3.14 DI3D – Definition BRIC Reinforcement** — definition of BRIC reinforcement (specific reinforcement strategy/model).
- **3.15 LAY – Definition of Multi Layer Reinforcement** — reinforcement definition for multi-layer configurations.
- **3.16 PARA – Design Parameter** — general design parameters.
- **3.17 PUNC – Punching Design** — parameters for punching shear design.
- **3.18 LC – Selection of Design Load Cases** — selects which load cases participate in design.
- **3.19 GRP – Selection of Groups** — selecting element/node/group sets for processing.
- **3.20 ELEM – Selection of Elements** — specifies which finite elements are included.
- **3.21 NODE – Selection of Nodes** — specifies which nodes are targeted (often for output or special checks).
- **3.22 SELE – Selection of Punching Points** — selecting punching check locations.
- **3.23 S – Input of External Forces and Moments** — provides external loading (forces/moments).
- **3.24 EXPO – Export of the Design Parameters** — controls export/output of computed design parameters.
- **3.25 ECHO – Control of Output** — controls verbosity/what output is produced.

### Interpretation for RAG retrieval
This table should be indexed as a **navigation and schema map** for BEMESS input: it links each **input keyword/group** (e.g., *MAT, GEOM, PUNC, LC, ELEM*) to its function and to a **documentation location** (page number range). In a RAG vector store, this is useful to retrieve “what does keyword X do?” and “where in the manual is it documented?” rather than to retrieve engineering calculation results.

 1 Task Description
 The program BEMESS is used to design forces of the analsis programs ASE or superimposed forces of MAXIMA according to various codes.
 It is also capable to extract extreme stresses from a set of loadcases according to the linear elastic theory.
 When the design is performed for several load cases, the result of the design calculation repre- sents the maximum reinforcement amount which is calculated from these load cases. BEMESS does not perform any load case superpositions. This is the task of the program MAXIMA.

It is also capable to extract extreme stresses from a set of loadcases according to the linear elastic theory.. When the design is performed for several load cases, the result of the design calculation repre- sents the maximum reinforcement amount which is calculated from these load cases. BEMESS does not perform any load case superpositions. This is the task of the program MAXIMA..
 Additionally to the ultimate limit design, serviceability checks can be done. This can be crack width control, minimum reinforcement, stress and fatigue checks.
 The compression reinforcement for shells and disks is calculated according to the stress state. The appropriate parameters are preset according to each code.
 For circular plates, cylinders or similar structures a circular reinforcement can be defined.
 The program performs a punching check at point supports (columns) as well as at wall corners and wall ends.

Special effects in a concrete shell design were published by SOFiSTiK on the Munich Concrete Seminar 2017. A short video shows the subject and different design strategies, see:
 YOUTUBE Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wIzO8YNLCn4
 The following design strategies have been compared:
 • Baumann design (SOFiSTiK since 1987)
 • Wood-Armer method (uniaxial design in 2 directions)
 • Capra Maury (uniaxial design every 5 degree)
 • Sandwich-Modell according EN-1992-2 attachment LL
 • SOFiSTiK Layerdesign (consistent iteration of strain)

 Also BRIC volume elements can be designed.

The image is a small schematic illustrating reinforcement behavior under skew tension in reinforced concrete slab/shell finite element design. It shows three separate blue reinforcement-mesh diagrams on a plain white background, separated horizontally and aligned at similar heights. Each diagram uses thick blue lines to represent a reinforcement mesh, and thin black arrows/labels to indicate force directions. The overall theme is how reinforcement responds when main stresses do not align with reinforcement orientation, leading to shear in the mesh and potential “rhomboid” deformation unless a compression strut in the concrete is present.

**Left diagram:** A square or orthogonal reinforcement mesh is depicted as a small grid of intersecting blue bars forming right angles. Two black curved/straight arrows with a label resembling “n-I” (partially cropped) appear near the lower-left edge, indicating a loading direction that is not aligned with the reinforcement orientation. This panel conveys a baseline orthogonal mesh subjected to a skew loading concept.

**Middle diagram:** Another rectangular mesh is shown, but it appears rotated or skewed relative to the loading arrows. The blue bars form parallelogram-like cells, implying reinforcement layers or mesh courses arranged so that tension is not acting purely along the mesh directions. Black arrows around the panel point in a direction that suggests a skew angle between the main tensile force direction and the reinforcement mesh.

**Right diagram (key concept):** The mesh remains blue and rectangular, but a red diagonal arrow and red outline indicate the resulting shear/skew tension interaction. A red diagonal line shows a direction of skew tension transfer through the mesh, producing deformation behavior. The reinforcement grid is drawn with one cell distorted relative to the orthogonal shape, suggesting deformation toward a rhombus (rhomboid) shape. This panel implicitly contrasts cases where reinforcement alone cannot carry the shear associated with skew tension; instead, the mesh tends to deform into a rhombic shape unless concrete compression struts provide an additional load path.

At the bottom of the image, there is a caption text in black: “Reinforcement mesh on skew tension, deformation to a rhomb, compression strut …” (the last words are truncated). There is also a visible black arrow label near the top center of the overall figure reading “n-I” (partly cropped). The arrows and caption together emphasize the mechanism: skew tension causes shear within the reinforcement mesh; without a concrete compression strut, the reinforcement cannot resist this shear and the mesh deforms toward a rhomb, whereas with a compression strut the mesh can carry the skew tension force.

In slab and shell elements the direction of the main forces usually does not fit to the direction of the reinforcement. The main stresses often load the reinforcement mesh with a skew angle. So a shear force appears in the reinforcement mesh. In case the concrete fails due to tension, the reinforcement allone cannot carry this shear and would deform to a rhomb. Only with an additional compression strut in the concrete the reinforcement mesh can carry the skew tension force, see the following figure:
 You can use an otogonal mesh or a three-course and/or skew two-course reinforcement mesh (record THRE). For circular plates a radial and a tangential orthogonal reinforcement can be selected through the input of a centre point.
 The program ASE determine the internal forces and moments in the local coordinate systems of the plane finite elements (see appropriate manuals). In BEMESS both the directions of the reinforcement layers and the terms ’upper’ and ’lower’ are oriented at the local coordinate
 systems; ’lower’ is at the side of positive z axis. Particularly in spacial systems the user should realize the characteristics of the local coordinate axis definition.
 The design of the necessary reinforcement cross sections occurs according to the material strengths and laws of the respective code.

The image is a schematic cross-sectional/planar diagram of a reinforced concrete member showing internal force flow and reinforcement layout. A light gray rectangular concrete domain is bounded by a black outline. Inside the rectangle, there are two adjacent blue diamond (rhombus) shapes, representing strut-and-tie type internal force paths or “meshes” aligned with reinforcement directions. The left diamond is centered slightly left of the middle; the right diamond is centered slightly right. The diamonds touch at a narrow crossing region in the middle, forming an overall two-cell arrangement across the width.

Within each blue diamond, a red vertical line is drawn near the left interior apex for the left diamond and near the interior apex for the right diamond. Each red line runs from the upper vertex of its diamond to the lower vertex, and the lines extend slightly toward the top and bottom edges of the concrete rectangle, emphasizing tension/compression force transfer along the reinforcement. At the mid-height of the figure, the blue diagonals form an “X” where the two diamonds meet, indicating that internal equilibrium is distributed among two reinforcement directions rather than along a single straight path.

A horizontal black arrow on the left edge points toward the diagram, and a matching horizontal black arrow on the right edge points away from the diagram, indicating an applied load or overall action direction across the specimen (likely a compressive/tensile global loading along the horizontal axis). Below the main diagram, there is a small caption-like text line: “compression strut (red) on 45 degree tension on the reinforcement mesh.” The red element is explicitly associated with a compression strut, while the blue reinforcement mesh (implied by the diamonds/diagonals) is associated with tension acting at a 45-degree orientation.

Overall, the figure visually supports the idea that, under a heterogeneous reinforced concrete stress state, the external loading is transformed into an internal force equilibrium system comprising: (1) compression struts in the concrete (shown in red) and (2) tension components carried by reinforcement arranged in a mesh-like pattern (shown in blue, with an indicated 45° tension angle). The two-course representation (two reinforcement directions) is depicted schematically, consistent with design discussions about orthogonal vs. skewed reinforcement and how internal forces align with reinforcement directions and concrete strut action.

In most stress situations the orthogonal two-course reinforcement mesh is the optimum solution of the design task.
 Skew two-course reinforcement meshes are chosen mostly due to constructive considerations. They are static generally less effective than orthogonal nets. The steel requirement increases more than linearly with the skewness of the reinforcement mesh. A two-course reinforcement is only allowed for 90 up to 60 degree skewness. For higher skewness a third layer is necessary to avoid large crack width.
 Three-course reinforcement meshes are the best statical solution for the case of an elliptic stress state (universal tension or compression): The required steel amount is minimal, i.e. it corresponds to the required cross section of an orthogonal reinforcement mesh laid parallel to the principal stresses. On the other hand there is no three-course solution for the case of the hyperbolic stress states (simultaneous tension and compression). For this a radically minimised two-course solution is sought. This is done via breaking off of this reinforcement layer which is used least statically. The stiffening compressive concrete force which generally must be assigned to another direction, however, is set at this place.
 The loading of the heterogeneous reinforced concrete continuum is transformed according to the compliance of the internal force equilibrium along the reinforcement directions (tension or compression) and the stiffening compression strut of the concrete (Figure 2.2).

In case the permissible compressive concrete stress is exceeded, a compression reinforce- ment is inserted if possible. The permissible compressive concrete stress is reduced in case of transverse tension - EN 1991-1-1 6.5.2(2). For lateral compression 100% are approved. In the region of 0.0 to 0.1 N/mm2 transverse tension the compressive strength is reduced linearly from 100 % to 80 % (or 75% according to the code). This reduction can be switched off with CTRL TENS 0.

The image is a schematic comparison of reinforced-concrete load-carrying behavior, shown side-by-side. It contains two main diagrams on a light background, each illustrating a column cross-section subjected to compressive forces.

**Left diagram (no CTRL PFAI 2 / constrained capacity):**  
A rectangular column cross-section is drawn in black outline and filled in light gray. Inside it, an “X”-shaped reinforcement pattern is visible: two diagonal blue lines form a diamond/rhombus shape, implying a reinforcement mesh oriented at approximately **45°** relative to the principal compression direction. Above the left column, a vertical arrow labeled **P** indicates an applied compressive load. Additional text to the right of the left portion includes the statement **“P > βc”**, implying that the applied load exceeds a concrete compressive capacity threshold parameter (βc). Near the top, the diagram suggests that the reinforcement mesh deforms in a way that prevents it from effectively bracing against tensile “splitting” behavior that concrete cannot carry, so the uniaxial principal compressive force cannot be fully taken up. The internal gray area and the blue reinforcement lines remain the focus; there is no red annotation here.

**Right diagram (with CTRL PFAI 2):**  
A second rectangular column cross-section appears in black outline with the same light gray fill and the same blue 45° diagonal reinforcement mesh forming a central diamond. Two vertical red boundary/triangle-like markings are visible near the lower portion (and along diagonal edges), suggesting additional force flow or load transfer zones. At the top, a compressive load arrow is shown again labeled **P**, and a nearby label reads **“P > βc”** and **“P > βc”** is emphasized. Importantly, the right diagram adds **red dashed arrows** and **blue/red force arrows** along the diagonals near the reinforcement, indicating that the load not carried by concrete is “transformed” into **compression forces in the compression reinforcement directions**. The text **“CTRL PFAI 2”** is placed to the right side of the diagram with a pointer to these indicated force paths. The overall visual message is that CTRL PFAI 2 changes the force distribution so that the same load can be carried even when only a 45° reinforcement mesh exists.

**Overall purpose / takeaway:**  
The figure visually contrasts the mechanism where concrete capacity is exceeded (left) leading to inadequate reinforcement action, versus CTRL PFAI 2 (right) enabling effective load transfer into compression reinforcement paths (with assumed support from neighboring elements). The principal geometry is a reinforced column modeled with 45° reinforcement mesh and vertical compressive loading P.

The image is a two-panel engineering sketch labeled “Figure 2.4,” comparing reinforcement behavior around openings/corners versus at wall-girder support locations, in the context of principal compressive force exceeding concrete capacity and the optional “CTRL PFAI 2” approach using compression reinforcement.

**Left panel (window opening – PFAI 2 useful):**  
A rectangular shell/plan area is drawn in light gray. Two thick blue horizontal lines represent orthogonal reinforcement mesh directions (one set horizontal, another set vertical). Two thick blue vertical lines are also shown, forming a cross-shaped grid. A bold blue line/axis runs vertically through the center of the rectangle. Red arrows indicate a principal compressive force state: a top-left-to-bottom-right red diagonal arrow points toward a critical corner zone, and additional red arrows show load transfer toward the area above a corner. A blue label at the top indicates “σ > βc” (compressive stress exceeding a limit). Near the top-left boundary, red text “σ > βc” is displayed with a red downward arrow and a red diagonal arrow suggesting that the concrete compressive force cannot be fully carried. Green arrows labeled “D” appear at the corner/critical regions to represent the portion of compressive force carried (or redirected) by compression reinforcement. The diagram also shows a green arrow pointing upward in the corner region, suggesting reinforcement is able to take over compression where concrete would fail, aided by load transfer/anchorage into neighboring elements.

**Right panel (wall girder support – PFAI 2 problematic):**  
Another gray rectangular area is shown, again with blue orthogonal reinforcement lines (a vertical blue line crossing a horizontal blue line near the bottom). A prominent red diagonal arrow points down toward the lower-right corner/edge, representing the principal compressive force direction at the support. The blue horizontal reinforcement line near the bottom ends at the right boundary, where a thin boundary/edge is visible, implying a free edge. An orange curved/angled marker labeled “(D)” is placed near the right side, indicating where compression reinforcement would need to act/where compression force would be directed. A vertical red upward arrow at the bottom-right boundary represents reaction or external loading. The key issue visually is that the compressive reinforcement direction required by the principal compressive force would point toward a free boundary, so anchorage and transfer (as assumed by CTRL PFAI 2) is not possible. The red diagonal load direction and the orientation of the blue reinforcement mesh make it clear that reinforcement cannot be properly braced/anchored at the required angle.

Overall, the figure contrasts an opening at a re-entrant corner (reinforcement can pick up compression and transfer it to adjacent elements) versus a wall girder support (required compression reinforcement would point to a free edge, making the method unsafe or problematic).

If the principal compressive force can not be carried by the concrete alone, the possibility of compression reinforcement must be checked.
 If reinforcement is available with a smaller angle, for example an angle with a 10 degree de- viation to the principal compressive force, then this reinforcement can take up a compressive
 force. The transverse reinforcement then gets a tensile force which can be interpreted as a splitting force. For the equilibrium of the external loads nx, ny, nxy with the inner forces of the concrete compressive force and the forces in the reinforcement directions it is now necessary, that the concrete compressive force is set a little bit skew (from the compression reinforcement away). Now the concrete compressive force is not in line with the external principal normal force. If the angle reaches 45 degrees between the new concrete compressive force and the principal compression reinforcement, then no further loads can be taken up anymore. Now it is not possible to design the cross section. Then the error message ’Angle between compressive force and compression reinforcement too large’ is printed.
 CTRL PFAI 2 can be used to alleviate this mechanically exact procedure and therefore to avoid the error message. The non absorbable concrete compressive force is then fully taken up by reinforcement without further checks of compatibility and it is assumed, that the compressive force of this inserted compression reinforcement is transferred to the neighbouring elements. Usually this is possible at singular points and at re-entrant corners, but not possible at free edges!
 To clear this effect following a column that is loaded uniaxially over βc. If only a reinforcement mesh on 45 degrees is available, also a high reinforcement can not hold the uniaxial principal compressive force, since the reinforcement mesh is deformed stressfree to a rhombus, see Figure 2.3 middle. To brace the reinforcement mesh a stiffening tensile force would be nec- essary but the concrete cannot carry that. On the right side the behavior with CTRL PFAI2 is shown. Here the same load can be carried because the force not be carried by concrete is just transformed inco compression reinforcement with the assumption that the neighbour elements can support this reinforcement compresssion.

To brace the reinforcement mesh a stiffening tensile force would be nec- essary but the concrete cannot carry that. On the right side the behavior with CTRL PFAI2 is shown. Here the same load can be carried because the force not be carried by concrete is just transformed inco compression reinforcement with the assumption that the neighbour elements can support this reinforcement compresssion..
 After this theoretical example now two practical ones. In Figure 2.4 a window opening is shown on the left. In case the concrete compression strength is exceeded in the element right above the corner, the reinforcement can help and carry a part of the loading. A compression force in the reinforcement in this element can be transfered to neighbouring elements and anchored there. So in this example an input CTRL PFAI 2 can help to design this singularity at the re-entrant corner using compression reinforcement.
 But in general this method is not allowed. E.g. at the support of a wall girder, the support compression would point to the support under 45 degree and the ortogonal reinforcement mesh could not carry additional compression. The horizontal bars point to a free boundary where a bar compression (D) could not be anchored. In this example the input of CTRL PFAI 2 would be wrong or at least problematic.
 The stress in the compression reinforcement is limited to a stress at 2 o/oo, that gives -400
 N/mm2 in most cases. Reason:
 In the shell design the forces are converted to a normal force in an upper disc and a normal force in a lower disc (Baumann method) - see Figure 2.7
 Then these discs are treaded as centric loaded parts and we limit the stress according EN- 1992.1.1 6.1 (5) to a stress at 2 o/oo.
 This is not exactly the meaning of the code but it is on the safe side.

Walls designed with BEMESS are considered always as ”reinforced walls”.
 A minimum reinforcement can be demanded, e.g. 0.8% of the statically necessary cross sec- tion (see record MAT ... AM3) . The minimum reinforcement calculation occurs in the direction of the principal stresses. The skew reinforcement is considered with the square of the cosine of the angular deviation.

The image is a screenshot from a structural analysis/design software (logo “SOFISTIK” at top). It shows a 3D concrete block representing a finite element, oriented in perspective, with embedded prestressing tendons and a stress/displacement annotation overlay.

Central object: A beige/yellow prism (the concrete element) with a right face (foreground) and a top face (upper plane). On the right side face there is a blue cylindrical/strip-like tendon depiction labeled visually as the “main tendons” direction. Near the right face, a blue shaded plane/region is marked “deco check,” indicating an area used for the decompression check in the design workflow. There is also a dark/black curved reinforcement line on the right side (near the blue tendon), suggesting an additional tendon bundle or reinforcement representation intersecting the face.

Top face details: On the top surface of the prism, a regular grid of small blue and red line segments indicates tendon layout and/or tendon-smearing geometry used for stress plotting and decompression/crack-related checks. Red arrows/markers are visible along the grid, likely indicating tendon directions (major tendons) and/or principal stress directions for the plotted result.

Legend / text overlay (left): A white panel contains stress/strain-like quantities in a monospaced style. The text includes:
- “top EC:” followed by min/max values expressed as “/oo” (per mille or percent-equivalent strain-like output), including negative and positive extremes (example visible: “min.ec = -0.613 0/00” and “max.EC = 0.052 0/00”).
- “bottom EC:” with additional min/max values (example visible: “min.ec = 0.318 0/00” and “min.es = -0.405 0/00”).
- “max. EURc” and “max. EURs” values (concrete compression and steel/tendon-related Eulerian/engineering stress measures are shown), including negative/positive maxima and minima.
- A computed formula-like term appears: “(min.ec = (e1I + p*e1)/(1-p^2)) in case of biaxial pressure” indicating the derivation used for biaxial pressure state.

Caption / figure label (bottom): “Figure 2.5: Tendons in decompression check.” Beneath/near the caption the panel indicates “Stress plot element 132 loadcase 2101 (loadcase with max. loading).” Thus, the visualization corresponds to a specific finite element (element 132) under a particular load case (2101) where the maximum loading is considered.

Overall, the figure is intended to illustrate tendon-induced decompression behavior: the model highlights the tendon direction relative to the right cube face for checking decompression, and it provides maximum/minimum concrete compression strains and tendon stress/strain measures for that element and load case.

The image is a schematic 3D view of a prestressed reinforced concrete structural element (likely a slab/beam segment) in the context of tendon effects on stress/shear. The scene is rendered in a light blue background with the soffit/geometry shown in a perspective view. A rectangular concrete member is depicted in white/gray with a visible top surface and side faces. Along the top, a set of blue longitudinal lines represent tendon ducts or tendon layout. Near the left end of the shown region, a circular or oval red-highlighted area marks a critical zone where effects (e.g., shear-related tendon duct reduction, stress transfer, cracking region, or an inspection location) are being evaluated.

Two directional axes are indicated: an “X” axis arrow points diagonally upward/right from the member, and “Vx” and “Vy” (in black) denote shear force components acting on the section. Specifically, Vx is labeled near the left portion with a downward arrow, and Vy is labeled near the right portion with a downward arrow. Beneath or adjacent to the member, “Vx↓” and “Vy↓” suggest shear actions with the two orthogonal directions. At the right side, a red/green rectangular block-like reinforcement or loading representation is partially visible, suggesting supports, end blocks, or localized shear connection components.

A blue arrow on the right indicates a shear or force direction, and the overall schematic emphasizes the relationship between the tendon duct location and the shear stress transfer. The red-highlighted circle draws attention to where the tendon duct reduction per code is relevant. The top view includes a striped/mesh-like pattern, reinforcing that this is a discretized or modeled slab region.

The included context text in the prompt references CSM/CSM Design parameters and checks (primary vs. secondary prestress effects, bonded tendon smeared width, CTRL SIGZ for switching tendon area contributions, CTRL LAY for SLS/ULS tendon strain checks, and storage/plotting of maximum concrete/tendon stress in a specific element/load case). This image likely corresponds to a shear design check involving prestressing tendon duct reduction (mentioned in the caption-like fragment: “tendon duct reduction in the shear design according to EN 1992-1-1 6.2.3 (6)”), with the highlighted circular region indicating the location where that reduction is applied relative to the shear stress components Vx and Vy.

The page shown is a technical documentation screenshot for the SOFiSTIK system (header “SOFiSTIK”, right-side title “Theoretical Principles | BEMESS”). The content mixes figure captions and explanatory text about prestress/tendon modelling options and checks in concrete design.

At the top, there is **Figure 2.5: “Tendons in decompresion check”**. The figure is a 3D block diagram of a concrete element (rectangular prism) with a **slab-like top surface** and a **bottom surface**. On the **right face** of the prism, there is a labeled **“Right face”**, and arrows indicate the **“main tendons”** direction pointing toward that face. The concrete is shown in pale yellow/cream with visible internal lines that represent cracks/strain paths. Over the top surface, a **grid of red dashed lines** overlies the element, representing the stress/strain plot mesh or reinforcement/tendon influence regions. sections: 2.2.7 Procedure of design according to Baumann (CTRL LAY 0)

content:
This reinforcement design is based on the method described by Baumann (Der Bauingenieur 47 (1972), pages 367-377). It looks a little bit similar to the sandwich-modell of EN-1992-2 annex LL.
 The moments m-xx, m-yy and m-xy as well as the membrane forces n-xx, n-yy and n- xy are converted to effective membrane forces acting on fictitious disks with a thickness of 0.35·construction element thickness at the outer shell side, see figure. The loading consists of force pairs divided up into bending moments and halved membrane forces. The lever arm of the internal forces required for the decomposition of the bending moments is not assumed according to BAUMANN. It is calculated at the basis of full utilisation of the compressive zone. For this the lever arm is determined for two characteristic directions (the principal bending mo- ment direction and the principal normal force direction). The smaller lever arm is used then for the segmentation of the moment into membrane forces.
 For approximately centrically pressed shells the cross section could not be used completely due to the limit of the equivalent thickness of 0.35·h. Therefore in this case the equivalent thickness is increased for centrically pressed shells up to the value 0.5·thickness·SC1/SC2. The 0.35·thickness is applied from an eccentricity e/d >0.20. For a smaller eccentricity it will be interpolated.
 The mesh reinforcement design occurs separately for the two fictitious disks at the shell/slab outer sides.
 Here once more the whole process: for each reinforcement layer aseparate lever arm is used:
 1. In the direction of the main bending moments as well as in the direction of the main normal forces the lever arm is calculated separately. The unfavorable laver arm is taken −→ leverarm z
 2. With this leverarm z the fictive disc forces Ax,Ay,Axy are calculated on the considered

content:
See also YOUTUBE Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i3dVC6tCSH8
 This method was completely new implemented in version 2018 and works with an exact itera- tion of the strain state. This method is called ’layer design’ in SOFiSTiK. It can also be used in the ULS design but it is not the default because it requires much more calculation time.
 In the layer design the 6 strain parameter (3 strains εx, εy, εxy and 3 curvatures κx, κy, κxy) are calculated iteratively to achieve equilibrium between the 6 inner forces and the 6 external forces nx,ny,nxy,mx,my,mxy. Thereby nonlinear work laws are taken into account for concrete and steel. Inside the reinforcement area no concrete stress is applied. On biaxial compression of concrete the poisson ratio is used. On uniaxial compression with transverse tension the poisson ratio is not taken into account, because the concrete only works uniaxial parallel to the crack. A further crack opening happens without poisson ratio effect. A concrete tensile strength is not taken into account - not even in the crack design as we are interested in the calculated crack width in the crack section.
 As all components are taken into account using the strain and curvature tensor, also the com- patibility is observed as in the Baumann design. So a tension force acting under 45 degree on a reinforcement mesh causes a necessary compression strut in the concrete.

$tope: minec = 0.037 o/oo maxec = 8.387 o/oo mines = 2.905 o/oo maxes = 2.987 o/oo ( minec = (epsll+y*eps!)/(1-u*2) in case of biaxial pressure ) topo: minoc = 0.0 MPa maxos = 435.6 MPa minos = 435.5 MPa bottom o: minoc = -19.8 MPa maxos =-119.5 MPa minos = -119.7 MPa bottom C/: minec = -3.500 o/oo maxec = -1.174 o/oo mines = -0.599 o/oo maxes = -0.597 o/oo cross direction or at least skew corfcrete compression Right face: stresses in direction of the max. main concrete compression strain Stress plot element 56 loadcase 9$.
 For the stress plot of the most forced element in a first check the maximum main concrete compression strain is searched (top or bottom). The stresses in this direction are shown at the right face of the plot cube. At the left face the maximum of the corresponding concrete transverse stress and a possible skew compression is plotted. This is favorable to recognize a skew compression strut stiffening the reinforcement mesh as the direction of main compression may turn over the height. The left concrete stress plot may also have a kink due to the effect that the poisson ration is only taken into account in case of biaxial compression!
 In case enough reinforcement is already defined coming from the ULS, the SLS procedure is relatively clear: with 6 target forces the 6 variable strain parameter are tuned. The iteration is controlled using a Chrisfield iteration method based on residual forces.
 In the ULS design the procedure is much more complex because a starting reinforcement is missing. In the beginning of the iteration the strains increase significantly, the cracked concrete cannot carry the loading. Then the program inserts reinforcement using panelty functions. An additional target appears to meet strain limits. If reinforcement is increased usually a strain limit of 25 Promille is the optimum. In case of compression problems at the compression face the tensile strain must be reduced. On further loading also compression reinforcement can be inserted to achieve equilibrium.
 Summary: Using the consistent strain iteration, the layer design can replace the up to now successful Baumann design. Mainly in the limit range of ULS design the layer design can deliver more accurate results.
 In the SLS the layer design delivers more accurate results than the up to now used uniaxial Capra-Maury method. Especially in post tensioned structures the Capra-Maury method cannot well map the real biaxial stress state.
 Tendons can now be integrated realistic in the strain analysis also in the analysis ot the lever arm (waste-product of the iteration of the strain state) - see tendons.

 Lever arm in the printout:
 A lever arm is not used in the layer design itself, only the balance of the internal stresses with the external internal forces is achieved. But for printing and information purposes a lever arm is extracted from the stresses. For this the center of gravity of the concrete compression stress is determined at the top of the section - see next figure left. Then the center of gravity of the iron tension on the bottom of the section is determined in this direction. The distance is then printed as lever arm ’zl’ = averaged lever arm of lower reinforcement. Should the concrete compressive strain transversely be more than 80% of the concrete main compressive strain at the top, the center of gravity of the iron tensile force at the bottom is averaged without direction, e.g. in the middle of a slab with m-I = m-II. The same procedure is then used for the main compressive strain at the bottom with the iron tensile force at the top for ’zu’ = averaged lever arm of upper reinforcement:

sections: 2.2.9 Sandwich design according new Eurocode prEN Annex G (CTRL LAY 2)

content:
If the new Eurocode is likely to be introduced in 2027 and the corresponding standard is then selected in Sofistik, the design in the GZT will then be carried out according to the new annex G. You can also activate this manually by entering STEU LAY 2.
 For stress analysis, layer design is always used as the default setting, as this provides much more accurate stresses. With the sandwich model, annex G only uses a rectangular stress block in the pressure zone. Crack detection is then carried out in the default setting using the Baumann design, which provides comparable disk cutting forces. However, the new calculation of crack widths according to Annex G.5 is used, which provides significantly higher crack widths than the old Eurocode, especially in corner areas of slabs with torsional moments mxy. You
 can also manually request crack evidence using this new method with RISS...SAND 11. See a1_single_span_girder.dat Singe span girder with 90 and 45 degree bars.
 Without normal forces and at mxy<0.07*dˆ2*fcd, the procedure is based on Table G.2 and uniaxial design according to 8.1.3 (works like the woodarmer method). Depending on the utilization of the pressure zone, the lever arm is optimally determined and the permissible steel tension is utilized up to the trilinear range of the working line. The design moments are stored - but are 100% identical to Baumann. A reduction in the concrete compressive strength does not take place according to Annex G, as this is only stated in Annex G.3 (membrane). A reduction according to 8.5.2 Compression struts and pressure fields is not necessary for plates. If the cross section cannot carry the force without compression reinforcement, BEMESS switches to SOFiSTiK layer design. As with the Eurocode shell model, the concrete compressive strength is also reduced for slabs. If necessary, BEMESS then attempts to achieve equilibrium with compression reinforcement.

A reduction according to 8.5.2 Compression struts and pressure fields is not necessary for plates. If the cross section cannot carry the force without compression reinforcement, BEMESS switches to SOFiSTiK layer design. As with the Eurocode shell model, the concrete compressive strength is also reduced for slabs. If necessary, BEMESS then attempts to achieve equilibrium with compression reinforcement..
 Shells:
 Even if a shell only has a small normal force, it is dimensioned according to G.3 (membrane). It also explicitly states that the steel stress can only be applied with fyd (G.1) - i.e. without a trilinear work law. In advance, the most unfavorable lever arm is determined for each iron using a simple woodarmer method, but with strength reduction on transverse tension. The MXY is added to the moment in the iron direction. But the NXY is added in such a way that it delivers a compressive force, because that provides the most unfavorable lever arm.

In case the minimum lever arm of all 4 irons (z-top-1,z-top-2,z-bot-1,z-bot-2, calculated with the woodarmer method) is greater than the center distance of the outer reinforcement layer, this center distance of the outer reinforcement is used. Otherwise the minimum lever arm of all 4 irons is used for the lever arm z of the sandwich disc distance according annex G figure G.2. This method with the outer reinforcement comes from the old Eurocode EN 1992-2:2005, Annex LL (informative)..
 The disk forces are then designed according to annex G, normally with fy/1.15 = 500/1.15 = 435 N/mm2.
 The concrete compressive strength on transverse tension is reduced according to annex G (G.9). If the concrete compressive strength is initially exceeded, BEMESS attempts to reduce the elongation eps1 by increasing the inserted reinforcement in order to increase the concrete compressive strength according to G.3(7)d). If the increase is more than 20%, BEMESS first tries to reduce the lever arm in order to increase the layer thickness t in order to reduce the concrete stress (more pressure zone, especially with normal pressure force).
 If the discs cannot carry the stress without compression reinforcement, BEMESS switches to the SOFiSTiK layer design. There the strain eps1 is not calculated with fyd according to (G.10) and G.4(7)a) but is determined exactly from the strain plane transverse to the compressive stress. If the reduction in compressive strength is high, BEMESS tries to limit it by reducing the steel elongation. You can also activate this new reduction in concrete compressive strength according to (G.9) according to old standards with CTRL TENS ’prEN’.

Up to now, the design of Steel fiber Concrete is only implemented according the german DAfStb-Richtlinie Stahlfaserbeton Ausgabe Juni 2021 and is used in this way also for other EN codes (a corresponding warnung is printed).
 - ULS bending design with the ULS worklaw from AQUA

 In case steel fibers cannot be used for a design, e.g. for the dynamic stress range, or if a check is not implemented, a corresponding error message occurs.
 You can then run an AQUA without steel fiber input in advance to get a normal check without steel fibers.
 After the plotted worklaws the tension stress points of the work law are printed. Example see steelfiberdesign.dat

Depending on the country, different boxed values are set. Important is the factor α-cc (fcd=α- cc*fck/γc). Please check the BEMESS material output!
 - Special values for v1 acc. 6.2.3(3) (6.10.aN)
 Important is here the additional safety coefficient gamma-n in dependence on the safety class (1,2 or 3). The safety class is defined in program AQUA via record NORM at CAT:
 NORM S BBK-04 CAT 1: gamma-n=1.00 CAT 2: gamma-n=1.10 CAT 3: gamma-n=1.20
 To change the safety class, an AQUA run with only an input for record NORM can be set in front of the BEMESS.
 - Bilinear material curve for reinforced concrete according to
 3.1.2-(3)P + 3.1.4-(3)P
 Concrete safety factor 1.90 [ with alfa-cd = 1.0]
 Crack check: in 4.4.2 it is recommended to reduce the steel stress accordning figure 31. This can be done in BEMESS with an input of PARA-SSO and a check with CRAC WK TAB. If the user inputs a specific crack width (e.g. CRAC WK 0.15), the analysis of crack width according EN-1992 7.3.4 is done. If this is not possible, shear reinforcement is in- serted. According SIA 262:2013, 4.3.3.4.3 the compression strud angle is analysed between 25 − 45◦.
 Hint
 Please note that in BEMESS, β = 90◦ → snβ = 1.0
 The concrete strength FC (Rb) and FCTK (Rbt) (see program AQUA record CONC) are re- duced with an additional factor for short term/long term loading that can be set with CTRL SNIP, default is 0.9 (long term loading). Steel is only used bilinear up to FY, for shear FP is used for Rs.

The concrete strength FC (Rb) and FCTK (Rbt) (see program AQUA record CONC) are re- duced with an additional factor for short term/long term loading that can be set with CTRL SNIP, default is 0.9 (long term loading). Steel is only used bilinear up to FY, for shear FP is used for Rs..
 According ACI 318-14 a strength reduction factor of 0.65-0.9 according Tabelle 21.2.1 is used, depending on the situation bending, bending+compression or compression alone.
 The strength reduction factor SRF is taken into account according to the table 2.3 AS 3600. bending SRF=0.6 - 0.8, shear SRF=0.7
If requested with the input, the following checks are performed after each other. If necessary the reinforcement is increased which is requested statically by the appropriate amount.

The check for a compression zone height can be done specially on slabs. In spacial systems with tensile normal forces the check usually failes in many elements because in the region of zero bending moment the sections are fully tension stressed.
 Therefore the check is done using a simple slab without normal force. Then the check gives a minimum reinforcement out of geometrical restrictions:
 Assuming a strain at the compression face, a well defined strain in the reinforcement appears using XMIN
 - With this strain in the reinforcement and the E-modulus of steel we get an allowable steel
 stress
 - With the concrete strain and the concrete E-modulus we get a compression force on XMIN
 - The reinforcement must carry this force with the allowable steel stress
 - The first assumed strain is cut away
 So the necessary minimum reinforcement is independant of the first assumed strain and only depending on the Geometrie and the ration of E-moduli.
 (Only CTRL LAY 0 uses the old method of BEMESS version 2016 - see manual of 2016)
 The check is requested with an input XMIN in the record CRAC.

content:
The check limits the available steel stress in the serviceability state to a permissible value. The permissible value comes from a code depending table depending on the bar diameter or
 can be input directly in PARA-SSU! With PARA-SSU a check can be done for the table of bar spacing! Usage:
 If a permissible steel stress is input via PARA-SSU, this value is taken. Otherwise the permis- sible steel stress is calculated based on the tabel bar diameter.
 If the check for the bar diameter table is not implemented vor a specific code, the check can always be done by direct input of the steel stress in PARA-SSU.
 It is assumed a crack formation through load. A crack internal force e.g. for a minimum rein- forcement must be requested in MREI.
 For thick plates the limit diameters are increased according to the standard. For arbitrary crack widths an interpolation inside the table is done.
 In the Baumann design CTRL LAY 0 tendons are not taken into account in the crack design. In the layer design a stress increase of bonded tendons is taken into account in the iteration of the strain state (can be switched off with CTRL SIGZ 0).
 In case a stress increase in bonded tendons occured in the tensile zone in the effective tension area Ac,eff, in the german DIN EN 1992-1-1 the steel stress of the reinforcement in this direc- tion is increased according (NA.7.5.3) - in all other codes not! In the crack design itself, for all codes bonded tendons in Ac,eff are taken into account according EN 1992-1-1 7.3.4 (7.10), in- dependant of 150mm rule of 7.3.2(3). This rule is written for the minimum reinforcement but for the minimum reinforcement tendons are not taken into account in BEMESS. The bond values are taken from 6.8.2 table 6.2.

content:
The image is a schematic diagram illustrating crack width design for *multilayer reinforcement* (reinforcing bars arranged in multiple layers through the concrete cover and depth). It is labeled **“Figure 2.12: Crack width design on multilayer reinforcement.”** The figure is composed of two main parts: a left conceptual bar/space representation and a right detailed mechanical/geometry sketch.

**Left section (layered reinforcement concept):**
- The left diagram shows a horizontal concrete element boundary (thin outline) with two reinforcement layer representations indicated by text labels.
- Two labels are visible inside the concrete block:  
  - **“as1 = 20cm²/2”** at the upper/outer layer zone (interpretable as reinforcement area per meter or per defined length for layer 1, split or averaged as indicated by “/2”).  
  - **“as3 = 10cm²/2”** at a deeper or inner layer zone (layer 3), also shown with “/2”.
- The left portion primarily conveys that reinforcement is distributed across layers, with different reinforcement areas in each layer (layer 1 having larger area than layer 3).

**Right section (geometry and stress transfer for crack calculation):**
- The right side contains a simplified cross-sectional model of reinforcement and stresses.
- A vertical steel/stress representation is drawn (thin black line) with a stress depiction near it labeled **“σ”** and a smaller stress label **“σ3”** associated with an inner layer region. Another stress label **“σ1”** is shown closer to the outer side.
- Distinct depth/position markers are indicated:  
  - **“d1 = 40mm”** shown near the right, representing the distance of the outer reinforcement layer from a reference plane (most outer reinforcement).  
  - **“d3 = 80mm”** shown further right/above, representing the depth to the inner reinforcement layer.
- A horizontal dimensioning line and arrows indicate the lever arm between layers and the location of the center of tension force. Small cross marks suggest discretization or crack spacing conceptual points.
- The diagram includes a note-like marker line pointing toward the reinforcement level positions (outer vs inner), emphasizing that crack width calculation depends on the effective depth and spacing related to reinforcement placement.

**Overall purpose and relevance to the provided context:**
- The figure supports the described computation method in multilayer reinforcement crack width design: different steel stresses in different layers (e.g., outer layer vs inner layer) and the concept of an *effective depth* (force center depth) used for crack width formulae.
- The schematic visually corresponds to the text context where layer forces are averaged and the center of tension is computed from layer contributions; it also matches the idea that the crack width calculation uses geometric parameters such as **concrete cover from the most outer reinforcement** and effective bar diameter/stress selection (maximum stress or force-center stress depending on program settings).

sections: 2.3.3 Crack Width Control with Direct Calculation

content:
If the simple check according to the tables is not sufficing, a direct calculation can occur with the default of the permissible crack width. For EN codes also equation 7.14 of EN 1992-1- 1 7.3.4(3) is taken into account (except Germany and Austria). If the check is not explicitly programmed in BEMESS for a specific code, the check is done based on eurocode. For this please check the protocol of the design parameters in the output.
 The method of direct calculation of crack width should be used especially in bridge design. For normal buildings, the limitation of the crack width without direct calculation according to the tables is recommended.
 In case of a LAY multilayer reinforcement, the layers are averaged with their force com- ponent. May be the most outer layer (d1=40mm) with as1=20 cm2/m has a steel stress of 200 N/mm2 und the next inner layer with same direction (d3=80mm) with as3=10 cm2/m has a steel stress of 140 N/mm2, the center of the tension force is at d-eff= 50.4 mm = (40mm*20cm2/m*200N/mm2 + 80mm*10cm2/m*140N/mm2)/(20cm2/m*200N/mm2 + 10cm2/m*140N/mm2). The crack width is then calculated according to the crack formulars with the (in the same way) averaged bar diameter. For the stell stress the maximum stress in this area is used. This is usually the steel stress in the most outer layer (can be changed with CRAC AIMA -10[mm] to the stress in the force center). To calculate the crack distance sr,max,
 the concrete cover c from the most outer reinforcement is used.
 The direct analsis of crack width is requested with an input WK PARA in the record CRAC.

The image is a technical diagram illustrating a concrete/structural plate or slab subjected to bending/shear loading and analyzed under a strain-state approach. The drawing is presented in a 3D perspective. The base structure is shown as a rectangular prism in light gray with slightly darker edges, representing a structural element (e.g., a concrete layer). On top of this prism, a planar grid is drawn in blue, consisting of parallel lines that intersect to form a mesh. This grid likely represents the discretization of the slab into elements or the set of design directions used in the stress-check procedure.

Over the blue mesh, three colored curved “strain” or stress trajectory/interaction lines are displayed. Two of these curves are green and intersect or overlap on the right side of the figure, and one is red on the left side. Each colored curve is thick and smooth, forming arcs that bow upward and then return toward the surface. Small arrowheads are visible along at least one curve, suggesting directionality (e.g., progression of strain vectors or principal strain rotation paths). The red arc appears to span diagonally across part of the mesh, while the green arcs focus more toward the right-center region.

A translucent black/gray circular or lens-like shape is visible near the right-center where the red and green curves converge, resembling a highlighted interaction zone. Near this region are numbered callouts “1”, “2”, “3”, and “4” in green and red/black, placed close to the arcs. The numbers indicate distinct points, regions, or strain/direction cases used in the Capra–Maury or substitute forced method. For example, “1” and “2” appear on the upper left and upper right of the convergence area; “3” and “4” appear to the right and lower right around where the green arcs reach.

Overall, the figure is labeled at the bottom-left: “Figure 2.13: Capra-Maury design.” This caption signals that the diagram specifically depicts the Capra–Maury design approach, likely showing how uniaxial strain states are iterated across multiple directions (e.g., in 5° increments, as referenced in the surrounding context). The visual emphasis on multiple arcs and numbered positions suggests that different uniaxial strain directions are mapped onto the slab surface to compute stresses and ensure equilibrium for the check method.

With NSTR various SLS stress checks can be done.
 Without input to CTRL LAY the SLS stress analysis uses the layer design with the mechanically consistent approach of the iteration of the biaxial strain state. This method does not use sim- plifications or modified analysis methods like Baumann or Capra-Maury but is based only on structure mechanical basics and the material work laws. Then all 6 forces nx,ny,nxy,mx,my,mxy are brought to equilibrium with the corresponding 6 strains in one iteration.
 With CTRL SLS V2 also the old methods can be set:
 V2=0 : SLS with substitute forced according Baumann
 V2=1 : uniaxial design every 5 degree according Capra-Maury
 In each element the stresses in concrete and steel are calculated for all loadcases with a uniaxuial iteration of the strain state in 36 directions (all 5 degree)
 V2=2 : mechanically consistent layer design (default)
 In the Baumann and Capra-Maury method tendons are not taken into account in the stress analysis. In the layer design a stress increase of bonded tendons is taken into account in the iteration of the strain state (can be switched off with CTRL SIGZ 0).
 In the layer design also the different bond behaviour of prestressing and reinforcing steel is taken into in the steel stress range according EN 1992-1-1 6.8.2 (6.64). For this tendons are taken into accound inside 2.5*d1 with d1=axis surface distance of the bar.
 With CTRL SIGZ 999 V2 0.45 the value xi (Ratio of bond strength between tendons and rein- forcing steel 6.8.2 table 6.2) can be set e.g. to 0.45. With CTRL SIGZ 999 V2 0 the increase of reinforcement stress due to tendon bond can be switched off.

The image is a schematic cross-section diagram illustrating shear force components in a “haunched” structural region (i.e., a section with a tapered or stepped thickness). The drawing shows a sloping structural member/plate bounded by two inclined planes, viewed in elevation or section. A vertical dimension line on the right indicates a thickness or height over the haunched zone, suggesting that the geometry changes along the member depth.

Along the inclined member there is a curved/slanted shear-force representation: two arrowed force blocks appear aligned with a principal shear direction. The upper force label is **Vccd**, shown as a thicker arrow (or vector) pointing along an inclined direction near the top of the haunch. Beneath it, the lower force is labeled **Vtd**, pointing along a similar but not identical inclined direction. The arrows are separated vertically, implying that the total shear action in the haunch is composed of contributions associated with compressive and tensile force components (inclined compression and tension forces).

Between the arrows, a small vertical notation line and a short bracket-like marker imply a relationship or transfer between the components (compression strut / tension tie contributions). The sketch includes a small black arrow (possibly indicating the direction of the shear parts) and a dashed/outlined rectangular arrowhead region to emphasize that these vectors are force resultants acting within the haunched region.

The bottom of the image contains a caption fragment with **“2.14: Shear force parts in a haunch”**, indicating that this figure is part of a technical manual or design description. Overall, the diagram communicates how the program decomposes shear into haunch-specific shear-force parts (compression/tension related), which are then combined in the shear check to determine the effective shear force for reinforcement design.

A shear check is performed for plates and shells. The critical shear force V is determined from the shear forces VX and VY as main shear force VED in this vector direction.
 In haunched sections die shear parts of the inclinded compression and tension force are taken into account. In the printout you then find VED as external force and VED* as shear force after the Vccd and Vtd reduction (or increase). The haunch reduction can be switched off with CTRL VLEV 0 V2 0.
 This shear force, divided by the lever arm of the internal forces (see bending design), results in the effective shear stress τ0.
 The output includes the shear zone, the existing shear stress τ0 and possibly the shear stress τ which has to be considered. Perpendicular links are assumed during the calculation of the required shear reinforcement. The shear reinforcement can be output in reference to an area (cm2/m2) or to the elements (cm2).
 The shear design according to EN-1992 and most modern codes is based on two design values of the sustainable shear force:
 • VRd,c:
 Design value of the sustainable shear force without shear reinforcement
 • VRd,m:
 Maximum design value of the sustainable shear force with shear reinforcement, which can be sustained without failure of the fictitious compression concrete strut. If this value is exceeded by the existing shear stress Vsd, the cross section can not be designed.
 If shear links are necessary, a minimum shear reinforcement is calculated according to the
 code.
 In BEMESS the method with variable compression strut inclination is implemented. The com- pression strut inclination is determined in this case according to the utilization degree.
 As VRd,cdepends on the longitudinal reinforcement, for first V>VRd,cthere are two possibilities - either compute shear reinforcement or increase longitudinal reinforcement to increase VRd1. This can be controlled with CTRL ro_v for the overall slab or with PUNC ro_v for punching regions. Example of an input ( bemess6_design.dat ):

As VRd,cdepends on the longitudinal reinforcement, for first V>VRd,cthere are two possibilities - either compute shear reinforcement or increase longitudinal reinforcement to increase VRd1. This can be controlled with CTRL ro_v for the overall slab or with PUNC ro_v for punching regions. Example of an input ( bemess6_design.dat ):.
 CTRL RO_V 0.5 $ The program attempts not to use any shear reinforcement $ up to this bending reinforcement ratio. The shear check $ increases perhaps the bending reinforcement up to this value. PUNC ro_v 1.50 $ for punching desing
 During the calculation of VRd,c and the compression strut inclination the available longitudinal tensile and longitudinal compressive reinforcement as well as the normal force to be included in the principal shear force direction are considered. Reinforcements are considered in this case with the square of the cosine of the angular deviation to the principal shear force direction.

Following boxed values are used depending on the code:
 - 6.2.2(1) Shear VRd,ct analysis
 - 6.2.3(2) max. compression angle cot0
 - No minimum shear reinforcement.
 - Minimum value for vrdc: vmn+k1*σcp according to 6.2.2(1) (6.3N)
 in normal shear design
 The shear design according to the old British Standard (not BS-EN1992) occurs like the check according to old EC2. The from the concrete alone sustainable shear stress v-c is determined in this case in dependence on the bending reinforcement in principal shear force direction according British Standard Table 3.9.
 Unlike the original EC2 the standard method in the shear design which shows a smaller shear reinforcement at weak loaded cross sections may not be employed here. The compression strut inclination beta is limited to 0.6 (according to B4700 equation 23).
 Shear design ass = γs · (τ-u-0.3ftj · k)/(0.9fe) max. shear stress 0.2fcj/γb or 5 MPa (compression strut)
 Plates without shear design are allowed to
 VSd ≤ 0.25 · ƒƒcd · r · (1.0 + 50 · ρ) · b · d · δ
 otherwise shear design with VSd ≤ Vcd + Vd with Vcd = 0.60fctd · b · d · δ max. shear force 0.3fcd· b · d minimum shear reinforcement min-Vd = 0.5 · Vsd
 In shear design, without increase of longitudinal reinforcement it is possible that bending rein- forcement plastifies, so an increased epsv acc. 4.3.3.2.3 (39) is used. Dmax is set to 32 mm. Value kc is set to 0.55 (4.2.1.7).

In shear design, without increase of longitudinal reinforcement it is possible that bending rein- forcement plastifies, so an increased epsv acc. 4.3.3.2.3 (39) is used. Dmax is set to 32 mm. Value kc is set to 0.55 (4.2.1.7)..
 In case the shear check needs longitudinal reinforcement up to ro_v (see ctrl ro_v) , equations 4.3.3.2.2 (38) and 4.3.3.2.1 are used. Then an elastic behavior of the longitudinal reinforce- ment is assumed as more than necessary longitudinal reinforcement is present. If this is not possible, shear reinforcement is inserted. According 4.3.3.4.3 the compression strud angle is analyzed between 25-45 degree. If shear reinforcement is necessary, a minimum shear reinforcement is used according 5.5.2.2 (110) (see 5.5.3.3). The maximum shear strength is checked acc. 4.3.3.4.6.
 For shear check of plates no shear reinforcement is used up to Qb according to equation (8.57). For this c is taken to 1.0·h0. On higher shear force, links are provided according to (8.58) with variable compression (c = 2.0·h0 , controllable with CTRL COTT). The minimum shear links are considered with qs ≥ 0.25·Rbt·b. The maximum shear capacity is limited with equation (8.55).
 The shear check is done according to the alternative model which is described in BBK 04-3.7.3.7. As for DIN-Fachbericht a minimum value vmin is used for the concrete bearing capacity. For the shear check the program attempts to increase the member resistance VRdc via an increase of the longitudinal reinforcement up to RO_V (see CTRL RO_V) in order to refuse a shear reinforcement. If a shear reinforcement is necessary, an optimal inclination compression strut is determined according to 3.7.4.3d. However, this compression strut inclination becomes not smaller than cot-teta≤1.5 due to BBK 04-figure 3.7.4.3b. If shear links necessary, they are designed to fs=fst according to 3.7.4.3f. A minimum shear reinforcement is not checked.

However, this compression strut inclination becomes not smaller than cot-teta≤1.5 due to BBK 04-figure 3.7.4.3b. If shear links necessary, they are designed to fs=fst according to 3.7.4.3f. A minimum shear reinforcement is not checked..
 In the shear design according ACI 318-14 a strength reduction factor of 0.75 for shear is used (ACI 318-14 Table 21.2.1). A minimum shear reinforcement is taken into account if necessary according ACI 318-14 Table 9.6.3.3.
 For shear design BEMESS tries to avoid, if possible, the shear reinforcement by increasing the longitudinal tension reinforcement up to CTRL RO_V.
 If this is not possible, for V>0.5*SRF*Vuc the shear reinforcement is designed with a variable concrete compression angle according to AS 3600 8.2.10. The minimum shear reinforcement is taken into account according to AS 3600 8.2.8. SRF is here the strength reduction factor (for shear SRF=0.7).
 - Without shear reinforcement: if τSd < β * τ0d according to 6.2.2(1) similar to EC2-vrdct
 - Otherwise full shear design with optimum compression angle via compression capacity acc. 6.2.2.1(14)P - (17)P
 - Minimum compression angle cot-theta: according to 6.2.2.1(9)(a):
 2.0 for curtailed reinforcement = default in BEMESS MAT-K1S
 2.5 if not curtailed: input in BEMESS-MAT-K1
 - Without minimum shear reinforcement for slabs (6.4.3.1 (4)P only for beams)

Load cases with support reactions have to be contained in the indicated load cases. If the internal forces and moments from the program MAXIMA are designed, the program BEMESS has to be informed also about the load case of the extreme support reactions (record LC). The use of boundary elements for linear wall support is the precondition for the automatic identification of wall ends and wall corners. An elastic edge support is recommended. The stiffness of this linear edge support results to c=E·D/h (with h=wall height) in this case and can be input generally with approximate 500000 kN/m for the usual building constructions. Indeed a PZ support with an additional output edge element is possible, however, high singular corner moments which depend on the element mesh strongly are calculated then at the re-entrant corners!
 The program searches then single support nodes (single columns) and wall ends as well as wall corners and performs a punching check for these points.
 The punching force at single support node uses the technique of connecting forces according Figure 2.21. At wall corners or edges a perimeter cut is analyzed, see section wall ends.
 Nodes with less than 5 kN support reaction are not considered! This has to be considered for the control of the punching points (with program WING ”QUAD ASPS SCHH 0.20”)! Within the punching area the plate shear design is replaced then by a punching check. The elements lying within this area get then at least the for the punching check necessary upper longitudinal reinforcement. If the bending design shows a higher longitudinal reinforcement, this becomes determinent. A normal plate shear design occurs outside of the punching area.
 Studrails: see PUNC KPU.
 In case of a column head the program verifies the punching in the inner and outer part. Exam- ple see bemess7_columnhead.dat.
 With ECHO PUNC EXTR a plot ot the punching sitiuation can also be requested if no shear reinforcement is necessary.
 So that a necessary shear reinforcement will not forget in the graphics, all points have the shear reinforcement in the punching area, also the points directly about the column!

For edge and corner columns the effective perimeter is reduced based on a segment method. In addition the punching force is increased by a beta factor.
 BEMESS determines itself the effective round cut automatically, when it is controlled whether in individual segments around the column blockouts or edges are to be found. It applies in this case individual segment areas like for the block load analysis. If for a segment area plate elements are used with 100%, the segment is considered as effective for the punching. Currently 72 segments are arranged with 5 degrees per segment. The search segments extend from dS/2 to dS/2+6·effective depth.
 In fig. 2.15 the segments 1,2+4 are not covered completely. Segment 1+2 finds the boundary, segment 4 finds the opening. The program can not differ between boundary and opening but the fact that two active segments u occur indicates that there must be an opening. Then the catched u is taken as the active perimeter. Without opening the active perimeter may be elongated up to the real boundary according EN 1992-1-1 figure 6.15. You find this in the full punching listing marked with ”+ boundary spacing”.
 The segment method delivers the effective perimeter u of the punching round cut. The ratio
 u/u0 is output in % in the result list.
 A column is considered as an inside column from 1.00·u0 to 0.80·u0., as an edge column from 0.80·u0 to 0.50·u0, as a corner column smaller 0.50·u0.
 In case a point lies exactly on the boundary we assume that this is only done to simplify the analysis model and the outer column face is alligned with slab boundary in reality. So the perimeter is elongated by 2*half column width in that case, see EN 1992-1-1 figure 6.15. In case the point lies a little bit inside the slab, the length of an exact perimeter at distance 2d is used.

In case a point lies exactly on the boundary we assume that this is only done to simplify the analysis model and the outer column face is alligned with slab boundary in reality. So the perimeter is elongated by 2*half column width in that case, see EN 1992-1-1 figure 6.15. In case the point lies a little bit inside the slab, the length of an exact perimeter at distance 2d is used..
 According to the standard the shear stress in the perimeter cut determined with u is increased with a beat factor for the rough consideration of not axisymmetric bending loading. Using CTRL WINT 0 the program calculates this eccentricity value beta according EN 6.4.3 (6.39). BEMESS extracts a restraint column bending moment also in case of a simple pz-supported slab using the shear force distribution around the punching node. If the column is really restraint with a rotational spring or a column beam the real restraint moment is used to calculate the beta value according EN 6.4.3 (6.39). The loadcase with the maximum product of Vz*beta will be designed for punching. This beta method is performed for all design codes - even if they do not note it explicitely.
 Usually we have a biaxial bending moment MX+MY. Thus also for international codes the extended german formula (NA 6.39.1) is used to combine both Mx and My. The function W1 according (6.40) is analyzed for the active part of the perimeter, also for edge and corner columns. In general the beta value is limited to 1.80 to avoid unrealistic high values. At edge and corner columns often high beta values are computed. But as the perimeter is already highly reduced at these columns, BEMESS uses the flat (approximate) values according EN 6.4.3(6)
 The beta value can also be set manually for every punching node with PUNC ... BETA but for security on edge and corner columns at least the flat value is used.

content:
Within the punching area the regular plate shear design is omitted and replaced by the punch- ing check.
 The high node moment in a singular supported node is reduced with delta-m = A/8·bmin/bmax (A = maximum support reaction, bmin, bmax = smaller, larger column dimension). It is con- sidered, that for biaxial moment loading (mI=mII) the support pressure can be determined only in each case to a half for a mI and a mII support moment reduction, therefore delta-mI= A/16 and delta-mII= A/16 for bx=by. The moment reduction is limited to max. 20 %. This reduction also works on switched off punching PUNC NO. With PUNC NO D 0.01 B 0.01 the moment reduction can be switched off. With SELE this can be switched off for specific nodes.
 In addition a larger thickness is used during the bending design of the central column node. In this case the thickness is increased from the column edge with 1:3. With the default of a plate thickness in the record GEOM as well as at wall ends and wall corners this increase does not occur. The increased thickness is printed in the case of ECHO REIN FULL per node.
 Legend 1 Load area Aod
 2
 determinant sections of the critical round cut Germany and Austria
 In case punching shear stirrups are necessary at wallends or wallcorners, a recommendation is printed to increase the force by 15 o/o for an external studrail design as shear forces also flow to the corner from outside the critical perimeter (passing the end of the critical perimeter). This increase is a SOFiSTiK own handling and can be switched off with CTRL WINT 0 V2 0.

Two wall segments are drawn in plan/cross-sectional style: the vertical wall segment (right) and the horizontal wall segment (left). An additional dimension line at the upper right shows “b” spanning the thickness or effective width of the vertical wall portion (or the perimeter segment length relevant to the load zone).
