Overall, the diagram communicates that at wall corners, punching shear assessment uses a defined punching perimeter segment length set according to \(1\cdot d\) (as suggested by the accompanying context text). It further suggests that the method for determining the punching force follows the same approach as used for wall ends, while highlighting that wall width has been decoupled/removed from the perimeter definition in the improved method.

The punching at wall corners was improved according EN-1991-1-1 and is also valid for other codes.
 At wall corners the side length of the punching perimeter is set to 1.·d (depending on the code). The wall width has no effect now! The analysis of the punching force used the same method than at wall ends.
 Legend 1 Load area Aod
 1

For EN-1991-1-1 codes the critical perimeter distance is searched iteratively. Other codes often use a distance 1.0·d . The distance to the slab boundary is not valued as critical as for normal slabs (the critical distance to the boundary is taken to 1.2-1.8·d depending on the slab thickness (6·d for normal slabs/openings). A higher boundary β value is then taken for a relation u/u0 < 0.95 (0.80 for normal slabs).
 Reduction of the soil pressure according EN-1991-1-1 is allowed with 100% area of the critical reduced design cut. PUNC LC_P reactivated to input a fixed loadcase for soil pressure reduc- tion. Futhermore now at least 90 % of the maximum soil pressure is taken for the reduction, also in case of lower minimum soil pressure, because usually the maximum punching force corresponds with maximum soil pressure (is not clear in priory).
 With ECHO PUNC 4 you can get the punchung force V-Ed without bedding reduction in the WINGRAF plot.

Depending on the code prestress normal stresses are taken into account for punching design, but only the part of real defined slab tendons crossing the punching zone. Normal forces of a normal 3D analysis without tendons are not taken into account!
 The vertical component of tendons is considered for the analysis of VED in all design codes. BEMESS searches for each punching perimeter the tendons which cross this perimeter. For a horizontal deviation of the tendon to the perimeter greater than 60 degree a tendon is not taken into account for this perimeter. Up to 40 degree the cosine is used, between 40 and 60 the contribution is interpolated. Creep and shrinkage are considered with a constant loss of CTRL VPDC - default VPDC=0.12 (=12%). With ECHO PUNC EXTR all used tendons are listed with their single effect.
 Instead of the automatic calculation of Vpd, Vpd can also be input manually for each punching node with PUNC...VPD (positive = relieving effect). The input value is then taken constant for each punching perimeter.

sections: 2.5.9 Punching Check at a Three-Dimensional System

content:
In increasing measure high-rise buildings are analysed according to the Finite Element Method also for three-dimensional systems. The singular column points and wall end points are a problem in the design especially for the shear design. The decisive punching points of column connections and wall ends are identified automatically also at inserted slabs and checked.
 Within a round cut the normal plate shear check can be omitted then. The bending moments are reduced at the columns. The decisive shear force results from the difference of the column forces over and under the slab. Because these parts are not anymore understandable from the column forces after a superposition with the partial safety factors, the punching force is integrated about the shape functions at the punching node from the bordering plate elements. The punching dimensions are extracted automatically from the column cross sections and the wall thicknesses.
 In the same manner a punching check is performed for columns and wall ends at elastic bedded
 foundation plates with deduction of the minimum soil pressure.
 In the illustration the automatically determined critical punching round cuts are plotted in red. Some punching points require multiple shear reinforcement perimeters. Here this is the case particularly in the foundation slab. The in each case reduced round cut is recognizable at the wall ends.
 The following Figure 2.21 shows how BEMESS calculates the punching force:
 Procedure: at the column node in the slab here 4 quad elements attach to the node. The connecting forces of these 4 quad elements are summed up and give the punching force.
 These connecting forces are much more precise that the quad shear forces that could be integrated in a perimeter around the column. Furthermore this method also works in case the column forces of a higher level are only applied as single loads. A problem is that usually only the MAXIMA superposed loadcases are used - see problemm of Figure 2.23
 A differnce of the column force above and below the slab is not used in BEMESS as the Max- Min column forces are separate results and sometimes not even analyzed.
 Punching is only performed on horizontal slabs but not at vertical walls!

**Left sub-figure (\(\gamma * g\))**:

**Right sub-figure (MAXIMA / extracted punching quantities)**:  
A similar column and footing appear, but now two arrows near the slab sides show the result of a MAXIMA superposition being concentrated into a punching representation. The left arrow is labeled “270” (downward), and the right arrow is labeled “200” (downward). To the right of the column, the figure explicitly states the extracted punching design results:

sections: 2.5.10 V-Ed analysis out of MAXIMA superposition loadcases

In the design of a normal slab or shell structure BEMESS only gets the MAXIMA superposition loadcases. The superposed support reactions don’t help because in a 3D system they do not give an information at the punching node. Lets now study an example, showing a slab on a column with dead load and wind. In a manual calculation you would check the combination γ ∗ g + γ ∗ and design punching with β ∗ V − Ed = 512kN:
 But the combination loadcase γ ∗ g + γ ∗ does not exist as a single loadcase in a normal analysis. There you only have the single loadcases and the MAXIMA superposition quad forces, e.g. min-mxx. From this BEMESS must extract a punching force and gets:
 The force V-Ed= 470 kN does not really exist but the design controlling value β ∗ V − Ed = 508kN is quite close to the manual value.
 Conclusion: the superposed MAXIMA quad forces can contain results from actions that cannot occur in parallel (left of the column force with wind, right of the column force without wind), but
 the design controlling value β ∗ V − Ed = 508kN is OK.
 Remark: by default BEMESS uses a minimum β of 1.15. So BEMESS would be on the save side here. To use the value β =1.08 you must input CTRL BETA -2.

The image is a schematic technical diagram illustrating the **control perimeter for punching shear** around a column in a reinforced concrete slab or footing.

On the left, a **rectangular slab panel** is drawn in **outline**. A **solid grey square/rectangular column head** (or support area) is placed centrally on top of the slab. The column outline is fully contained within the slab outline. Around the column, a dashed **rectangular “critical/control perimeter”** is shown, positioned at a distance **related to the effective depth**. The key vertical and horizontal distance callouts include **“d/2”** near the slab, indicating the reference location where shear stresses or checks are taken (i.e., a control perimeter at a distance proportional to the slab thickness/depth parameter).

The left side also includes the labeled **dimension “b”**, likely representing slab thickness or a geometric parameter of the member/plate. At the bottom, the formula for the control perimeter is printed:
- **u = 2·a + 2·b + dV/2 · π** (the expression is partly constrained by resolution, but it clearly shows a perimeter length composed of **two times each side dimension (2a and 2b)** plus a **π·(something involving d/2 or d·v/2)** term corresponding to **rounded corners** or a sector approximation. The diagram suggests that the perimeter is not purely rectangular; it has **corner arcs** (indicated by the circular/curved representation implied by the π term).

On the right, a **zoomed cross-sectional view** focuses on a **corner region** (or a segment of the control perimeter). A **circular/annular arc** is drawn, with a grey shaded interior representing the slab region, and a dashed boundary indicating the **distance from the column face to the control perimeter**. The label **“d/v2”** (interpretable as **d/2**) is shown along a radius-like direction from the column-support region to the curved control line. This reinforces that the control perimeter includes **curved portions** at the corners rather than only straight lines.

Overall, the figure communicates: **punching shear is assessed along a control perimeter located at a distance “d/2” from the column/support area**, and the corresponding perimeter length **u** is computed by combining straight sides (2a + 2b) with an additional **arc/corner contribution** captured by a **π term**.

The image is a schematic cross-section/plan-view diagram illustrating the **reduced control perimeter** used for **punching shear** verification around a column support in a reinforced concrete slab or footing. The key visual elements are:

- A **thick, rounded-corner square/rectangular boundary** representing the outer extent of the considered slab area (or the region of interest).  
- Inside this boundary is a **darker inner gray zone** that represents the **basic control region** or the area within which punching shear is considered.  
- The gray zone contains **four curved, dashed-like arc shapes** near each side, visually indicating how the **control perimeter is affected by geometry**, especially around corners of supported areas. The arcs suggest that the perimeter is not simply a straight line but includes curved segments related to the punching layout.
- A **small solid/corner marker** at the top indicates a reference point for the control perimeter location and demonstrates where the reduction concept applies.

Two key **dimension annotations** are shown:
- Along the right side, there is vertical text indicating **“1.5·dv”** (likely a distance multiple relevant to the control perimeter definition).  
- Near the bottom-right and right margin, additional arrows and text indicate **distance multiples such as “1.5·dv” and “d·v”**-style notation, consistent with punching shear design distances measured from the column face and/or within a critical region around the punching perimeter.

The caption at the bottom clearly states:
- **“Figure 2.25: Reduced control perimeter u”**  
This identifies the drawing as part of a method where the **effective punching control perimeter \(u\)** is reduced under certain conditions (e.g., when the basic control perimeter would otherwise exceed a limit, such as \(> 12d\), as referenced in the accompanying context text).

Overall, the figure communicates that, depending on slab support geometry and distance limits, the **perimeter used to compute punching shear stress** is reduced, and this reduction includes effects from **corner contributions** (curved arcs near corners) rather than assuming a fully regular rectangular perimeter.

The image is a technical drawing showing the concept of a *reduced control perimeter* \(u\) for punching shear calculations (shown as Figure 2.26). The diagram contains multiple schematic cross-sectional views of a reinforced concrete support/plate scenario with a central concentrated action (e.g., a column). The key focus is the geometry of the control perimeter used to evaluate punching resistance and shear stresses around the critical region.

**Left schematic (rectangular support / reduced perimeter):**
- A gray block represents the supporting element (likely the column or concentrated load area) embedded in or connected to a surrounding concrete slab.
- A dashed, rounded-rectangular line encloses the gray block. The line indicates the *basic punching control perimeter* or a modified (reduced) perimeter path.
- Several dimension markers and arrows indicate offsets from the loaded area:
  - On both left and right sides there are labels “\(b\)” with arrows pointing outward from the central block edges, indicating a width component or an offset parameter.
  - On the top and bottom there are diagonal arrows labeled “\(1.5 \cdot d_v\)” showing the extension of the control perimeter beyond the loaded area by a factor of the effective shear depth parameter \(d_v\).
- Beneath the sketch, the reduced control perimeter length is expressed by a formula:
  \[
  u = 2 \cdot 1.5 \cdot d_v + b + \frac{d_v}{2}\cdot \pi
  \]
  The expression combines straight segments (from the \(2 \cdot 1.5 d_v\) term), a rectangular width component \(b\), and a curved contribution (the \(\frac{d_v}{2}\cdot \pi\) term), suggesting that the perimeter includes a circular/rounded portion.

**Right schematic (edge-related reduction concept):**
- Another partial schematic appears at the right side of the figure, showing only part of the support and slab boundary (suggesting proximity to an edge or corner).
- A vertical boundary line indicates a slab edge or limit, with dashed lines showing how the control perimeter would be truncated or modified when the punching perimeter reaches/approaches the edge.
- A “\(1.5 \cdot d_v\)” label appears near the truncated region, again indicating the same distance from the loaded area to the control perimeter location, but constrained by the edge condition.

**Overall:**
- The figure emphasizes that the control perimeter for punching shear can be reduced compared to an unbounded case, with the perimeter consisting of straight and curved segments and being further altered when near edges.
- The use of the parameter \(d_v\) (instead of \(d\) in the provided context text) indicates a slab shear-depth-related dimension used for the punching control geometry in the referenced SIA/figures described in the context.

The program BEMESS uses the CADINP input language, see general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’. Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The table is a configuration/definition index that lists **input record types** (left column) and the corresponding **parameter “items”** (right column) that may appear within each record. It is oriented to a structural/FEA model input workflow where an **arbitrary record order is allowed**, but with a strict rule that **END must always be the last record**. Furthermore, it states that **ELEM** and **NODE** records trigger the creation of a design using **already defined parameters** (with defaults if not specified). Any subsequent records such as **GEO**, **DIRE**, or **THRE** after an **ELEM/NODE** are interpreted as applying to the **next design**.

The table enumerates the following record categories and their item lists:

### 1) **CTRL**
Contains global or design-control settings. Items listed include:  
- **TYPE, TENS, WARN, RADP, RMOD, LCR, LCRI, BUBB**  
- **SYSt (SYST), PFAI, VF70, REDM, PFAL (as “PFAI”), VPDc (VDC/VBDC-like code), SIGZ, LCRP**  
- **WALL, A UGM (AUGM), COTT, FACH, SNIP, WINT, WEND, REDN, WTR? (W T EN), W R E N (as shown), THIC**  
- **RO_V, SNIP, VPDc, SIGZ**  
- **FCT, KC, K, PARA, K1** and additional parameters like **LCRP, WETN (as shown WTen)**  
Overall, CTRL appears to parameterize how the structural installation behaves (e.g., orientation/sections/constraints), including sizing factors and warnings.

### 2) **CRAC**
Defines cracking-related settings. Items include:  
- **MU/EZ, XMIN, DDES, STAN, WK, BET A (BETA), BOND**  
- **BET1, BET2, K1, DDEx (DDEB), WKB, MUEZ**  
- Parameters for model behavior under cracking/load scenarios.

### 3) **MREI**
Modifies cracking or stiffness properties related to reinforcement/element behavior. Items listed:  
- **FFCT, KC, K, PARA, ROBU**  
This suggests multipliers/coefficients for reinforcement stiffness evolution.

### 4) **SHIFT**
A simple record for shift parameters:  
- **TYPE** only (indicates what shifting method/definition is used).

### 5) **NSTR**
“Number/string/state” type record for structural state definitions. Items listed:  
- **SIGS, SIGT, CHKC, CHKR, FATC**  
- **LS_U, LS_L, LS_V, LS_P, FACU, FACL, FACV, FACP**  
- **LOCP, SIGP**  
This group defines threshold-like values and factors governing strength/stress limits.

### 6) **MAT**
Material property record(s). Items listed include:  
- **CONC** (concrete), **STE E** (steel), **K**, **BETZ**, **N**, **MINC**, **MSTA**  
- **T011, T02, T03, AM3, FC, FY, TU0**  
- **TUGR, TRD, SC1, SC2, SS1, SS2**  
So MAT defines concrete/steel parameters, strength coefficients, and additional scaling/limit parameters.

### 7) **GEOM**
Geometry/specimen dimensions and derived measures. Items listed:  
- **H, HA, DHA, HB, D H B, DDHA, DDHB**  
- **HPRE** (preparation/height-related parameter)

### 8) **DIRE**
Direction/axis orientation definition. Items listed:  
- **UPP, LOW, TYPE, X, Y, Z**  
This indicates the coordinate direction vector or axis orientation for the subsequent design parameters.

**General note from the caption/context:** the records **HEAD**, **END**, and **PAGE** are handled specially and are described in a general manual (“FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics”). The table itself primarily serves as a **catalog of valid record types and their associated keywords** so the parser/engine can apply the correct defaults and interpret parameter applicability across ELEM/NODE designs.

This table is part of an input-definition system where structural “designs” are assembled from a sequence of record types. It defines how the parser should interpret records and how parameter sets are applied across multiple designs. The “input sequence” is arbitrary in order, but with one critical constraint: the record **END must always be the last input record**. The table further explains that **HEAD**, **END**, and **PAGE** follow a general description in the manual *SOFiSTiK: “FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics”*. Therefore, these control records govern overall document structure (start/end/page handling) rather than defining engineering parameters.

The record types **ECHO**, **OPT**, and **VAL** are explicitly mentioned as “records defined.” While the table excerpt does not provide their internal field definitions, it clarifies their role in the input stream: they participate in defining and evaluating subsequent data or design behavior. Typically, in such systems, records like **ECHO** manage output verbosity or echoing input, **OPT** applies options or toggles, and **VAL** provides values for variables/parameters; however, the exact semantics are not included in the provided excerpt and should be interpreted in conjunction with the full manual sections for those records.

A key rule governs parameter inheritance: **each “ELEM” or “NODE” record triggers the creation of a design** using the parameters that have already been defined (either explicitly in the input or via **default values**). The excerpt states: “Each ELEM or NODE record causes a design with the already defined parameters (possible as the default values).” This means that as the reader processes the file, it accumulates parameters from prior records; when an element or node definition is encountered, a new design instance is instantiated using the current parameter context.

Additionally, the table explains the effect of record ordering around **GEO**, **DIRE**, and **THRE**. Specifically, if a **GEO / DIRE / THRE** record appears after an **ELEM/NODE** record, it does **not** modify the already-created design; instead, it “refers … always to the next design specifications.” In other words, GEO/DIRE/THRE records are buffered for the next ELEM/NODE-triggered design, ensuring clear separation between geometry/direction/threshold parameters for successive design instances.

Finally, the table notes that a “reasonable analysis is possible even without data” because defaults are activated “in each case.” This implies the configuration system is robust: if certain parameters are omitted, the software falls back to predefined default values rather than failing or leaving undefined states. The phrase “Table continued on next page” indicates this excerpt is part of a larger table; field-level details for ECHO/OPT/VAL and the precise parameter list for the designs are likely provided in subsequent pages.

The table enumerates **record types** used by a SOFiSTiK-style input interface. Each “Record” (e.g., THRE, PARA, PUNC) groups a set of **keywords (“Items”)** that are valid within that record. The document context indicates that only **three records are pre-defined**: **ECHO**, **OPT**, **VAL**. The table also clarifies sequencing rules: although the order of records is arbitrary, **END must be the last** record in the input. Each occurrence of **ELEM or NODE** initiates a “design” using already defined parameters, while subsequent geometry/direction/thickness specifications (e.g., GEO, DIRE, THRE) apply to the *next* design specification after ELEM/NODE. Additionally, **HEAD, END, and PAGE** are governed by the general manual section “FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics”.

### Record groups shown in the table

**1) THRE / DI3D / LAY / PARA / PUNC**
- **THRE** includes parameters/choices: **ABEX, ABMI, ABIN, BEEY, BEBI, BEIN** (set of abbreviations likely tied to thickness/three-dimensional setup or related option families).  
  It also provides coordinate components **X, Y, Z**, suggesting THRE may define spatial orientation or geometry-related reference axes.
- **DI3D** lists **OAL, OAF, X, Y, Z**, reinforcing 3D geometry/orientation definition.
- **LAY** contains **POS, Z, DIRE, D, AS, ASMA, BS**, implying “layer” positioning and directional descriptors.
- **PARA** defines a larger parameter block with quantities such as **NOG, NOEL, DU, DU, DU3, DL, DL2**, plus families **DL3, WKU, WKU2, WKU3, WKL, WKL2, WKL3**, and **SSU, SSU2, SSU3, SSL, SSL2, SSL3, ASU, ASU2, ASU3, ASL, ASL2, ASL3, BSU, BSU2, BSU3, BSL, BSL2, BSL3**, and **TYPE**. This indicates THRE-based design parameters with multiple variants for “upper/lower” or “layer/zone” thickness/width-like properties.
- **PUNC** provides point-related or punch-related data: **TYPE, X, Y, Z, D, B, HEAD**, plus additional parameters **DHEA, RO_V, MREI, P, LC_P, REIN, L**, and **VPD, RO_M, RO_L, MMOM, HRED, BETA**.

**2) LC / GRP / ELEM / NODE / SELE / S**
These records appear to structure *connectivity/selection* and *grouping*:
- **LC**: **NO, PERC, FACT**  
- **GRP**: **NO, ENVA, ENVB, WKU, WKL, SIGU, SIGL**  
- **ELEM**: defines element ranges/sets using **FROM, TO, DElt (DELT), WKA, WKB, SIGA, SIGB**.
- **NODE**: similar range/set specification: **FROM, TO, DELT, GROU, WKA, WKB, SIGA, SIGB** (note: repeated/overlapping keyword families across ELEM/NODE).
- **SELE**: **NO, TYPE**
- **S**: selection coordinates/values **NO1, MX, MY, MXY, VX, VY**, and index-like **NX, NY, NXY**, implying mapping of a selection to parameter pairs or coordinate-like dimensions.

**3) EXPO / ECHO**
- **EXPO** supports **OPT, TO, PASS**, controlling an “exposure/exponent/operation” behavior with options and a transfer/processing target (**PASS**).
- **ECHO** supports **OPT, VAL**, aligning with the earlier context that **ECHO/OPT/VAL** are among the predefined record controls.

Overall, the table serves as a **keyword index**: it tells which **items are allowed under each record label**, covering (i) 3D and layer/thickness-like configuration (**THRE, DI3D, LAY, PARA**), (ii) point/definition parameters (**PUNC**), and (iii) selection and association with elements/nodes/groups (**LC, GRP, ELEM, NODE, SELE, S**), plus (iv) control/echo/execution options (**EXPO, ECHO**).

Each ELEM or NODE record causes a design with the already defined parameters (possible as the default values). An input of GEO or DIRE or THRE after ELEM/NODE refers thus always to the next design specifications.
 The records HEAD, END and PAGE are described in the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’.

### Table description: `NORM` / design-code selection and related parameters (SOFiSTiK)

This table defines the **design code (“NORM”) configuration** for a record, including optional **country/variant selection**, **category/class selection**, and some **geographical inputs** that can influence environmental action parameters. It also documents how SOFiSTiK uses these inputs to choose defaults from internal **INI-files** (configuration files located in the SOFiSTiK directory).

---

## Columns / fields represented

- **NORM** (Design code family / standard selector)

The table defines control parameters for a reinforced-concrete design program (SOFiSTiK context) that govern the **design task selection** and the **saving mode** for computed results. It is organized into columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. Two main items are shown: **TYPE** and **RMOD**. An asterisk (*) in the default column indicates that the default value depends on the system or is not fixed in this excerpt.

---

## Item: TYPE (Design task)
**Unit:** LIT  
**Default:** * (system-dependent)

TYPE selects what type of calculation/design operation the program performs for the given load cases. The table lists the following allowed modes:

- **ULTI**: *Reinforced concrete design for load cases on ULS level*.  
  Additionally, it specifies that for **load cases on SLS level**, an averaged safety factor can be input via **LC FACT**.

- **ACCI**: *Reinforced concrete design for accidental design situation*.

- **EARQ**: *Reinforced concrete design for earthquake design situation*.

- **SLS**: *Serviceability limit state (SLS) design checks*.  
  The table indicates that this corresponds to or triggers checks such as **→ MREI, CRAC or NSTR** (i.e., crack/deflection-related serviceability criteria depending on the referenced modules).

- **STRE**: *Linear stress calculation according to the theory of elasticity*.

The description notes: **default** behavior for TYPE is “in dependence on the system,” meaning the program decides the baseline task unless TYPE is explicitly set.

---

## Item: RMOD (Save mode for reinforcement or stresses)
**Unit:** LIT  
**Default:** * (not fixed in excerpt)

RMOD defines how results—specifically **reinforcement distributions** and/or **stresses**—are handled in terms of storage during calculation runs. Options:

- **SING**: *Single analysis, no save*.
- **SAVE**: *Save does cover newly computed values but does not include any additional stored maximum*.
- **SUPE**: *The maximum of the calculated reinforcement and previously stored reinforcement is saved*.  
  This is intended for scenarios where multiple analyses are performed and the governing reinforcement should be retained.
- **DELE**: *Delete* (it references **see CTRL LCR**), indicating deletion of previously stored reinforcement/stress data controlled elsewhere.

It also states the default saving behavior explicitly:
- **default:** **SAVE in ULS, SUPE in SLS**  
  Meaning: under ultimate limit state design, results are stored without taking a max against prior values, whereas under serviceability design, the program keeps the most demanding (maximum) reinforcement outcome.

---

Overall, this table is a **configuration selector**: TYPE determines *what structural design calculation* is performed, while RMOD determines *how computed values are stored/combined across runs*, enabling either simple overwriting, maxima accumulation (critical for multi-case designs), or deletion/no-save modes.

So the external shear force VED must be lower than VRDbbbe = 0.55*VRDc of a full section. The output VED/VRDm then means VED/VRDbbbe and can be checked in WINGRAF-VED/VRDm. Additionally, within punching perimeters, also the normal shear check will be performed for bubble elements.
 Example: see bubble_deck.dat
 BOUN - Shear design at supports
 Without further input now the shear force in case of direct support is linear reduced from the face of the support up to xVED*d = controlling shear cut at xVED*d (see. DIN 1045-1 10.3.2(1) and EN 1992-1-1 6.2.1(8)). The value xVED is set according to the design code and is proto- colled in the output. It it set to 1.0 for EN, DIN 1045-1 and all new EC codes, otherwise 0.5. With CTRL BOUN V3 ... the value xVED can be changed.
 To satisfy EN-1992 6.2.1(8) ’Any shear reinforcement required should continue to the support’ the shear force it not reduced linear to 0 % (Version 2016) but to 70 % at the support face. This factor can be input with BOUN V2 - default Voreinstellung CTRL BOUN 1+2+4 V2 0.7.

To satisfy EN-1992 6.2.1(8) ’Any shear reinforcement required should continue to the support’ the shear force it not reduced linear to 0 % (Version 2016) but to 70 % at the support face. This factor can be input with BOUN V2 - default Voreinstellung CTRL BOUN 1+2+4 V2 0.7..
 $$For the check of VRd,m the shear force is linear reduced only from the support axis up to the face of the support = check at the face of the support (DIN 1045-1 10.3.2(3) and EN 1992-1-1 6.2.1(8)). From the face of the support up to the controlling shear cut VRd,m is checked with the unreduced shear force.$$
 CTRL BOUN can controll:
 BOUN 0 no reduction - shear design also over the support
 BOUN +1 at supported edges the shear force is reduced from the face of the sup- port up to xVED*d (direct support)
 BOUN +2 also at shell edges with walls below (slabs in 3D-high-rise building)
 BOUN +4 also at vertical shell edges (wall corner in 3D-systems - mostly indirect support)
 BOUN +8 also at all other shell edges (slaps hanging on walls ... - indirect supports)
 (shell edge = intersection of two parts, e.g. wall/floor or wall corner)
 At shell edges of type +4 and +8 indirect support is assumed and the shear force is reduced only in the intersection zone (support axis up to the face of the support). T beams in slabs gen- erally are takes as a direct slab support (support width = beam cross section web thickness).
 Default:
 1+2+4 = at direct supports and vertical edges.
 3.4.1 CORE Parallel computation control
 SOFiSTiK supports parallel computing for selected equation solvers. Additionally, some pro- grams offer parallel element processing capabilities – independent of the chosen equation solver (CTRL SOLV).
 By default parallel computing is triggered automatically where it is feasible.
 Parallel computing requires corresponding hardware and operation system support. In addi- tion, availability of an adequate SOFiSTiK license is obligatory.
 Hint
 Parallel computing requires availability of a HISOLV license (ISOL granule).

Additionally, some pro- grams offer parallel element processing capabilities – independent of the chosen equation solver (CTRL SOLV).. In addi- tion, availability of an adequate SOFiSTiK license is obligatory.. Hint. Parallel computing requires availability of a HISOLV license (ISOL granule)..
 If parallel computing is active, the number of adopted threads is determined as follows (listed with increasing priority):
 a) The software retrieves the information about the number of available physical processor cores on the system. This number defines the default number of threads that are used when a parallel computation is activated.
 b) This default can be modified via the environment variable SOF_NUM_THREADS, which is also available as sofistik.def parameter.
 c) Finally, an explicit statement CTRL CORE NN (or as relative input CTRL CORE NN[%]) temporarily assigns the number of available threads for the respective run.
 Hint
 Neither option b) nor option c) state an explicit parallel computation request. The deci- sion if a parallel computation is triggered, depends on the actual analysis option (parallel processing must be supported for the specific task) and the availability of an adequate license. Parallel computing can be suppressed by explitly setting the number of available threads to 1 (or 0).

The input table describes parameters for **crack-width verification** in a reinforced concrete (RC) member. It supports two main crack-check modes: a **simple crack width check** using tabulated limits and steel bar spacing, and a **precise crack width check** using direct calculation (e.g., **DAfStb-Heft 400** or **EN 1992-1-1**).

### Key fields and meanings
- **CRAC (block identifier)**: Enables crack-width analysis. The table is “continued on next page”, indicating more parameters follow elsewhere.
- **Item Description – XMIN**: “Minimum thickness of compressive zone.”  
  Notes: Not possible with the **Baumann design** or in **multi-layer reinforcement**. It is only meaningful for **slab systems**, where a compressive zone thickness assumption affects crack width.
- **WK**: “Computed crack width value.”  
  Used as an output/parameter to control crack checks. Also supports special behavior: **WK = 999** triggers “analysis of crack width” (direct calculation interpretation).
- **TAB**: “Check of diameters with tables via GRP + ELEM + NODE > 0.”  
  Indicates that crack-width verification is driven by **predefined bar diameter/spacing tables**. It relies on environment and recorded geometry through **GRP, ELEM, NODE** selections.
- **PARA (parameter input source)**: “BOND Indicator of exterior surface quality” via rebar/concrete bond quality factors:  
  - **RIB** = ripped concrete steel  
  - **PROF** = shaped concrete steel  
  - **PLAI** = smooth concrete steel  
  These map to **beta factors** in the crack formula.
- **BET1**: Coefficient **β1** in the crack-width formula for **wk**. It reflects bond properties. Default mapping stated:  
  - **RIB → 1.0**, **PROF → 0.75**, **PLAI → 0.5**.
- **SILO analysis related parameter**: “SILO analysis for silos with” a specific effective-height expression:  
  \( sr,max = 2*c + \frac{1}{2*1.8} \cdot \frac{d}{ro,p,eff} \)  
  Any numerical value can be entered otherwise, implying this table can be used for specialized silo geometries.
- **BET2**: “Input for load duration.”  
  - **SHOR** (short time loading): implies **BET2 = 1.0** (Heft 400) or **kt = 0.6** (EN 1992-1-1).  
  - **STAT** (long term): implies **BET2 = 0.5** (Heft 400) or **kt = 0.4** (EN 1992-1-1).
- **WKB**: “Computed crack width value for lower side,” with a default unit **[mm]**. Shown entries suggest defaults like **1024 = 0. [mm]** and **1026 = LIT … → WK**, implying indexed table rows/IDs control parameter activation.
- **Special option “-8 for Denmark 2023-3”**: Indicates a regional design-code variant affecting crack-width calculation.

### Control logic: simple vs precise crack checks
- **Simple crack width check**: Crack limits are checked using **table-based steel stress limitations**. Controlled by **DDES** and **WK = TAB** through environmental conditions or explicit crack width from **PARA** or from records tied to **GRP / ELEM / NODE**.
- A special workflow is described: if **steel stress** is manually provided via **PARA-SSU**, the system checks against table bar spacing by extracting the corresponding steel stress from the relevant table. If steel stress is not defined for an element, it is designed using **table bar diameters**.

- **Precise crack width check**: Activated when **PARA** is provided or when **WK** is set in record **CRAC**. In this mode, **concrete tensile stress (BETZ)** from **MAT** must not be set (it can be zero). The parameters **WK to K1** are used only for the precise check.
- **CRAC CODE**: Allows crack analysis for another **EN country code**.
- **AIMA option**: Used to compute **effective height** \( (h-d)/3 \) variants for crack width:  
  - **AIMA 140 mm** sets \( aimax \) directly.  
  - **AIMA = 999** uses a computed distance from outer to most inner reinforcement + \(0.5\Phi_{i,max} + c_{-inside}\).  
  - It then defines  
    \( hc-eff = \min\{2.5(h-d), h/2, \max[(h-x)/3, aimax + 0.5\Phi_{i,max} + c_{outside}]\} \).  
  This can **increase calculated crack width**.
  - **Negative AIMA values**: keep \( hc-eff \) unchanged but alter steel-stress assumptions (sandwich-like equilibrium using the tension-force center level). **AIMA = -999** can further increase \( hc-eff \) but note explicitly: negative AIMA leads to **significantly lower crack width** than positive AIMA or no AIMA.

Overall, the table is an expert configuration for crack-width verification, combining **surface quality/bond (BOND/BET1)**, **load duration (BET2)**, **optional geometry adjustments (AIMA)**, and **mode selection (simple tabulated vs precise direct calculation)** with special handling for silo analysis and regional code variants.

sections: 3.6 CRAC – Control of the Service Load Checks

content:
The table defines configuration inputs for a crack-width/steel-stress verification workflow (in the CRAC-related functionality). It has four columns:

1) **Item**: the parameter name to be set in the calculation (e.g., `SAND`, `AIMA`, `CODE`).  
2) **Description**: what the parameter controls, including the meaning of numeric codes/options.  
3) **Unit**: engineering unit or notation for how values are interpreted.  
4) **Default**: the default value used when the parameter is not explicitly provided.

---

## Parameter: `SAND` (crack-width interaction model selector)
**Unit/Default**: shown as “–” (dimensionless option), with **default = 0**.

**Meaning**: `SAND` selects how reinforcement “interaction” is accounted for in slabs using **EN 1992-1-1:202** (as referenced in the text). The entries are discrete numeric modes:

- **0**: no additional strain interaction terms are added (no `esmx−ecmx` and `esmy−ecmy` contribution; described as “version before 2023-6” behavior).  
- **1**: adds strain interaction terms `esmx−ecmx` and `esmy−ecmy`, but only if the difference between `f?m` and `f?l` is **< 5%** in midspan of a four-sided-supported slab (a “threshold” rule).  
- **2**: like mode 1, but the transition region is broader: **2.5%–7.5%**.  
- **11**: similar to 1 but “as 1 but plus le2/ lacc… (G.26)” and described as leading to “harder, gives jumps in midspan.”  
- **12**: similar to 2 plus the same additional `le2/lacc` per (G.26).  
- **-1**: described as “as 0 but without limit of crack width with factor 0.9”; crack-distance `s_r,max` may be reduced “too much” otherwise (the text explains a special caution for default). It notes that with this mode the **0.9 crack-width limiting rule is not applied on SAND > 0**, and summarizes how the 0.9 limit is generally treated in EN 1992-1-1 (7.15), including behavioral differences in `SAND=0` versus `SAND>0`.

Overall, `SAND` is an **EN modeling switch** that changes how strain interaction between reinforcement layers (x/y directions) influences crack-width results.

---

## Parameter: `AIMA` (effective height adjustment option)
**Unit**: **[mm]** and default shown as “-” (not fixed in the snippet; the input is optional).

**Meaning**: `AIMA` sets or modifies the **effective height** used in the crack-width computation (the table explicitly says “option to calculate the effective height (see below)”). The supported behavior is:

- **Input a positive value** (example shown: `AIMA 140 [mm]`): then `aimax = 140 mm` and the effective height is computed via  
  `hc-eff = MIN{ 2.5*(h-d) ; h/2 ; MAX[(h-x)/3 ; aimax + 0.5*Φi,max + c-outside] }`.  
- **Special value `AIMA = 999`**: `aimax` is defined algorithmically as the **distance from outer to the most inner reinforcement + 0.5*Φi,max + c-inside**, where `c-inside` is based on inside cover and related to outside cover handling.  
- **Negative `AIMA` (e.g., `AIMA = -10 [mm]`)**: `hc-eff` remains unchanged, but the **steel stress level is taken differently** (similar to a sandwich model), using the stress distribution referenced to the center of the tension-force level to satisfy equilibrium.  
- **`AIMA = -999`**: may also increase `hc-eff`.

The description includes a key warning: **negative `AIMA` tends to produce significantly lower crack widths** than positive `AIMA` or no `AIMA`.

---

## Parameter: `CODE` (international country code selection)
**Unit**: displayed as `[LIT]` (integer code).  
**Default**: “–”.

**Meaning**: `CODE` chooses which **EN country code** is used for crack-width calculations. It maps integers to regions/standards:
- `1` = Original EN  
- `2` = German  
- `3` = BS  
- `4` = Italy  
- `7` = Austria  
- `8` = Denmark  
- `9` = Netherlands  
- `10` = Norway  
- `11` = France  
- `12` = Belgium  
- `13` = Sweden  

A note in the text mentions a “special option” for Denmark (2023-3), tying back to the broader CRAC/ENV behavior.

---

In summary, the table is a parameter catalog for crack-width checks, where **`SAND`** governs reinforcement interaction behavior, **`AIMA`** modifies or redefines the effective height/steel-stress assumption for the “precise” crack-width calculation, and **`CODE`** selects the country-specific EN variant used to compute crack width.

The table lists key input items used for the **minimum reinforcement (MREI)** check according to **EN 1992-1-1: 7.3.2** (minimum reinforcement for crack control), including an additional “robustness reinforcement” concept. It is part of a larger design parameter/data structure where values are provided through an “MREI” record (and related records such as **FFCT**, **KC**, **K**, and **ROBU**).

**Columns**
- **Item**: Short identifier used in the input data.
- **Description**: Human-readable meaning of the parameter.
- **Unit**: Unit field, shown as “–” for all listed items, indicating the parameters are dimensionless coefficients or flags/values used directly in formulas.
- **Default**: A default value is not provided (blank in the screenshot). Therefore, the user is expected to supply meaningful values or rely on program-specific derivations described elsewhere in the context.

**Items and their technical meaning**
1. **FFCT** – *Factor for effective tensile strength*  
   This parameter scales the concrete’s effective tensile strength for crack-related reinforcement calculations. Per the surrounding context, the effective tensile strength factor is used like:  
   \[
   f_{ct,eff} = FFCT \cdot f_{ctm}
   \]
   For lightweight concrete, the text indicates a minimum choice of **FFCT = 1.0** (leading to **fct,eff ≥ 3.0 N/mm²** as stated).

2. **KC** – *Coefficient for stress distribution during first cracking*  
   This coefficient governs how stresses are distributed at the onset of cracking, affecting the minimum reinforcement calculation. The context states that if **KC is not entered**, the program determines it from axial force for 3D systems, and also gives reasonable suggested inputs depending on boundary conditions, e.g.:
   - Bending constraint: **KC = 0.4** (with **FFCT = 1.0**, **K = 1.0**)
   - Centric constraint (e.g. hydration heat): **KC = 1.0** (with **FFCT = 0.5**)

3. **K** – *External constraint factor (depth-dependent)*  
   This parameter represents external constraint effects, “for bending constraint usually input with K = 1.0.” The context also states that **K is calculated depending on depth**; and for **external constraint** such as column settlement or bending constraint, **K = 1.0** should be used.

4. **ROBU** – *Robustness reinforcement*  
   This parameter enables an additional check ensuring ductile member behavior (“minimum reinforcement for safety of a ductile member behavior”). The context explains that the check is performed using:
   - **fctm** when using **MREI ROBU FCTM**
   - **fctk** otherwise, with the possibility to override tensile strength via **ROBU** (example: **ROBU = 2.50 N/mm²**).  
   It further states that robustness reinforcement is always applied at the **bottom**, and on the **top only when tensile stresses occur**, typically over up to **one quarter of the span**.

**Overall interpretation for use in RAG**
This table summarizes the dimensionless/core parameters controlling EN 1992-1-1 minimum reinforcement calculations (crack control via effective tensile strength and cracking stress distribution) and an optional robustness reinforcement check. Since defaults are not specified in the table, correct calculation relies on user-provided values or on automatic derivation rules described in the accompanying text.

MREI
 The minimum reinforcement according to EN 1992-1-1 7.3.2 is defined with the record MREI FFCT, KC and K. In Germany the increase of hc,ef acc. figure 7.1d is taken into account. A tendon reinforcement is not taken into account, the MREI crack moment is calculated into a necessary normal reinforcement.
 The factor of the effective tensile strength results as follows:
 ƒct,eƒƒ = FFCT · ƒctm
 Minimum 3.0 N/mm2 (leightweight concrete) are used for FFCT = 1.0.
 Without an input for KC the coefficient is determined from the axial force for three-dimensional systems. Reasonable inputs are:
 MREI FFCT 1.0 KC 0.4 K 1.0 for bending constraint MREI FFCT 0.5 KC 1.0 for centric constraint from hydration heat
 The item K is calculated in dependence of the depth. For external constraint (column settlement or bending constraint) it should be input with k=1.0.
 The determination of the minimum reinforcement requires an input of the crack width WKU and WKL in record GRP respectively in the design parameter dialog! For a parallel explicit crack width input in CRAK WK (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.4), this is used also for the minimum rein- forcement. If the limitation of the crack width according to tables (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.3) is desired simultaneouslywith CRAK WK TAB, WKU and SIGU can be input in record GRP (or the design parameter dialog)! Then WKU is used for the minimum reinforcement and SIGA is used for the limitation of the crack width without a direct calculation according to tables (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.3).
 Example: see bemess6_design.dat

If the limitation of the crack width according to tables (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.3) is desired simultaneouslywith CRAK WK TAB, WKU and SIGU can be input in record GRP (or the design parameter dialog)! Then WKU is used for the minimum reinforcement and SIGA is used for the limitation of the crack width without a direct calculation according to tables (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.3).. Example: see bemess6_design.dat.
 ROBU: the check of a minimum reinforcement for the safety of a ductile member behaviour (ro- bustness reinforcement) occurs with an input for ROBU. With MREI ROBU FCTM the check is performed with the concrete tensile strength fctm, with MREI it is performed with fctk. However, a different tensile strength may be input with ROBU, e.g. MREI ROBU=2.50 (N/mm2).
 The minimum reinforcement is then calculated according EN 1992 9.2.1.1(1) equation (9.1N). Only for german design codes a crack moment is calculated and designed with a fixed lever arm value kz=0.9 and the steel yield strength fyk according (NDP) 9.2.1.1 (1). The robutsness reinforcement is always applied at the bottom of a section. On top only in case of appearing tensile stresses. To recognize this it is necessary to define a permanent loadcase for this check may be with a little factor only, e.g. LC (2721 2726 1) FACT 0.001. Usually the robustness reinforcement on the top has to be placed over a length of up to a quarter of the span length.
 Varying MREI input for different groups is not possible in one run, but you can make multiple PROG BEMESS runs with different GRP selection.

The input table defines a parameter for a structural design feature related to the “shift rule,” where an offset value is optionally considered in calculations. The table has four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. It contains one configurable setting named **TYPE**.

### Table structure
- **Item**: Indicates the name of the parameter being configured.
- **Description**: Explains the meaning of each possible value for the parameter.
- **Unit**: The unit is given for completeness; in this case it is not applicable because the parameter is categorical.
- **Default**: Specifies the default value used if the user does not override it.

### Parameter: TYPE
- **TYPE** (Unit: “–”, Default: **0**) controls whether and how the software considers an **offset value for the shift rule**.
- The table provides two allowed modes:
  1. **TYPE = 0**  
     - **Description:** “0 does not consider”  
     - Interpretation: the model does **not** take the offset value for the shift rule into account. In other words, the shift-related adjustment logic that depends on an offset is disabled or ignored.
  2. **TYPE = 1**  
     - **Description:** “1 Consideration according to EC 2 method”  
     - Interpretation: the model **does** consider the offset value, using the methodology aligned with **EC 2** (Eurocode 2). This implies that the shift rule’s offset handling follows EC 2 assumptions or computation steps.

### Engineering context (from provided SHFT text)
The accompanying context explains the physical meaning of “SHFT” as a mechanism where applying **SHFT = 1** results in an **additional normal force** that causes a **shift in bending reinforcement**. It further notes that near supports (up to approximately **0.5 · z · cot(θ)**), the **shear force is reduced**, and that the program adjusts the **minimum compression strut angle** (default **CTRL COTT 7/4**) to avoid unnecessary longitudinal reinforcement increase in midspan.

In terms of the table, **TYPE** acts as the switch that determines whether such an EC 2-consistent offset consideration for the shift rule is applied. When **TYPE = 1**, this aligns with the broader “SHFT” behavior where reinforcement shifts and shear redistribution occur according to an EC 2-based approach.

content:
The table describes input parameters for **fatigue/stress-range checks** and related **reinforcement increase controls** in a slab/concrete design workflow. Each “Item” corresponds to a specific stress range quantity that can be provided to the program (often by defining or triggering a check). Units are given explicitly and the “Default” column provides system behavior when the parameter is not overridden.

### Columns
- **Item**: Parameter mnemonic (e.g., `SIGS`, `SIGT`).
- **Description**: What the parameter means and how it affects calculations (including default assumptions and reinforcement behavior).
- **Unit**: Engineering unit for the parameter values.
- **Default**: Default value or default behavior (including dependence on other inputs).

### Parameter meanings and behavior

#### `SIGS` — Stress range of longitudinal reinforcement
- **Unit**: N/mm²
- **Default**: “-” (no fixed numeric default stated in the table, but behavior is defined relative to other inputs)
- **Function**: Defines the stress range for longitudinal reinforcement for fatigue-related checks.
- **Reinforcement update logic**: The program will **increase reinforcement if necessary**.
- **Special note**: `NSTR SIGS 999` is treated as a mode that **checks the stress range only** (no reinforcement increase).

#### `SIGT` — Stress range for shear reinforcement
- **Unit**: N/mm²
- **Default**: `0.454*SIGS`
- **Function**: Sets the stress range used for shear reinforcement fatigue checking.
- **Default rationale**: The default is derived from longitudinal stress range due to **small bending diameter** assumptions.
- **Reinforcement update logic**:
  - Reinforcement is **increased if necessary**.
  - **Punching shear reinforcement is not increased** due to this check (important for scope limitation).
- **Special input**: If `SIGT` is provided as a **negative value**, the system forces a shear stress range calculation in shear reinforcement such that **shear reinforcement is generated in every element**. This enables comparison to see whether the required shear reinforcement is smaller than an imposed minimum (the minimum itself cannot be input “up to now” per note).

#### `SIGP` — Stress range for prestressing steel
- **Unit**: N/mm²
- **Default**: “-”
- **Function**: Target stress range for prestressing steel fatigue behavior.
- **Coupling to reinforcement**: The program runs **BEMESS** checks to achieve this stress range by **increasing longitudinal reinforcement**.
- **Failure mode**: If the target cannot be met, a **warning occurs**.

### Concrete/steel stress limits and control switches

#### `CHKC` — Maximum concrete compression stress
- **Unit**: “– , N/mm²” (the hyphen indicates special enumerated modes plus numeric input capability)
- **Default**: `0`
- **Modes**:
  - `0.45`: enables a check against **0.45·fck** (“Check to 0.45 fck”).
  - `0`: disables control (“No control”).
  - `>1.5`: interprets as a **direct numeric limit in N/mm²**.
- **Reinforcement behavior by layer design context**:
  - In layer design (default on `NSTR`): reinforcement will be **increased if necessary and possible**.
  - With `CTRL LAY 0` (Baumann): reinforcement **won’t be increased** (check-only behavior).
  - With `CTRL LAY 1`: a pure check without increase can be done via `NSTR CHCK -0.45` (negative value indicates check-only variant).

#### `CHKR` — Maximum steel stress
- **Unit**: “– , N/mm²”
- **Default**: `0`
- **Modes**:
  - `0.8`: check against **0.8·fyk**
  - `0`: no control
  - `>1.5`: direct limit in N/mm²
- **Reinforcement behavior**: Unlike check-only modes in concrete, the table states plainly that **reinforcement will be increased if necessary**.

#### `DECO` — Check distance for decompression check
- **Unit**: `[mm]`  
- **Default**: `1011` (as shown; likely a formatting/placeholder artifact from the source—should be interpreted as the default mm value)
- **Function**: Sets the **check distance** used for the decompression check (fatigue/decompression related) for the region above and below the duct surface.
- **Context from provided notes**: The program normally reads the default from an `.ini` file; `NSTR DECO 120[mm]` is allowed to override it without the typical `h/10` limitation.

### Overall workflow implication (from the surrounding notes)
These `NSTR` items feed **stress range computations** over defined load cases (often involving LC permutations and permanent load factors). For `SIGS` and `SIGT`, the computed stress ranges are used to decide whether reinforcement needs to be **increased**; certain magic values (e.g., `999`) or negative/CTRL settings enable **check-only** behavior. The table thus functions as a configuration interface for fatigue-related stress range limits and reinforcement update control.

The input table (continuation) appears to define **NSTR-related fatigue and stress-range control parameters** used in a structural design workflow for prestressed concrete slabs. It mixes short parameter identifiers with descriptive guidance on how the software performs checks and how user inputs influence reinforcement updates, stress range computation, and graphical outputs.

### Key rows / fields

- **NSTR (fatigue age of concrete / not used / legacy)**
  - A row explicitly notes: **“FATC – Fatigue age of concrete FATC. No longer used, please.”**
  - This indicates that the program previously supported a fatigue-age parameter but has deprecated it. The table also shows placeholder entries (“-”, “-”) where legacy options likely existed but are now inactive.

- **FATC and material fatigue definition**
  - Another row states that fatigue-related material input is defined as **“fcd-fat” in the material**, referencing: **“see AQUA CONC FFAT”**.
  - It notes an alternative or related restart mechanism: **“Also possible as AQUA-Restart see AQUA CTRL.”**
  - This implies fatigue design strength parameters are controlled indirectly via material settings, not via the deprecated FATC input.

- **REST (context only)**
  - The table includes the token **“REST”** without an immediately visible detailed description in the snippet, suggesting it is another configuration keyword for the NSTR-related process.

- **G_SD (gamma-sd for fatigue to LC14)**
  - **“G_SD – gamma-sd fatigue to LC14.”**
  - It references **EN1992-2 (NN.112)** and mentions a mismatch: while EN1992-2 writes **γ_sd**, the software expects **γ_Ed,fat**.
  - A critical note warns: **“Attention: Using SIGS, SIGT, CHKR, LS_U, LS_L, LS_V, FAKU, FAKL or FAKV, the reinforcement will be increased to fulfil the check.”**
  - This establishes that gamma-related fatigue parameters are tied to the stress-range/fatigue design logic, and that certain user inputs can trigger reinforcement increases.

### Stress range computation logic (NSTR / SIGS / SIGT / DECO)

The table’s description text documents algorithmic behavior rather than numeric columns:

- **NSTR SIGS**:
  - Used to verify the **stress range of reinforcement**.
  - Process outline:
    1. Run a “normal design” with possible serviceability checks.
    2. Consider an already saved reinforcement state at **“CTRL BMOD SUPE”**.
    3. For each load case, compute reinforcement stresses.
    4. Take **minimum and maximum across all load cases** to form the final stress range.
  - Restriction: **only 100% permanent factor** is allowed for the NSTR load case setup (explicitly described via “LC...PERC used for other checks”).
  - Requires pre-generation of load cases with/without live-load parts using **MAXIMA**.

- **ECHO options**:
  - **ECHO NSTR FULL** prints elements that require **no reinforcement increase**.
  - **ECHO SIGS NSTR** outputs stresses per single load case and the used updated lever arms.
  - A two-step behavior exists when running **CTRL BMOD SUPE** after an earlier stress-range-controlled calculation: the second run may yield smaller stress ranges because reinforcement increased previously is reused (i.e., the system controls reinforcement increase consistency).

- **SIGT (shear link reinforcement stress range)**:
  - For shear link stress range **(SIGT)**, the **square route of strut inclination** is used per EN1992-1-1 6.8.2(3) (6.65).
  - The software checks whether shear direction alternates across load cases (decompression indicator).
  - Special feature: input **negative SIGT** (e.g., **-120**) forces calculation of a shear reinforcement stress range and triggers shear reinforcement **in every element**—primarily to compare against minimum shear reinforcement that cannot be input up to now.
  - Note: stress range is **not used for punching checks**; over punching nodes, shear reinforcement is not increased due to SIGT.
  - For graphical checks, a link stress range based on the real slab shear force is stored for **WinGRAF**.

- **DECO (decompression check distance and strain storage)**:
  - **DECO** governs decompression check per EN1992-1-1 7.3.1.
  - Default check distance is **100 mm** from an `.ini` file, adjusted to the design code.
  - User can override: e.g., **NSTR DECO 120[mm]** (no h/10 limitation).
  - On each stress check with NSTR, maximum decompression strain above/below tendon duct surfaces is computed and stored for **WINGRAF**.

### Fatigue check control

- Fatigue of **concrete** is controlled via **LC14** (with optional additional input to LC14 plus a permanent load case).
  - It computes **σ_c,perm** and a parameter **λc0**.
  - A “simple check” is also performed for comparison.

- Fatigue of **steel** is activated if the user provides at least one of: **LS_U, LS_L, LS_V, FAKU, FAKL, FAKV**.
  - **SIGS** is defined per **DIN-FB 102 4.3.7.5** or **EN-1991-1-1**, with SGS expressed as **ΔσRsk(N*)**.

### Practical interpretation for RAG

1. **Which fatigue/stress-range keywords exist** (NSTR, FATC legacy, REST, G_SD, SIGS, SIGT, DECO, LC14, LS_* and FAK*).
2. **How inputs change computational behavior** (reinforcement increases, stress range determination across load cases, special shear handling).
3. **Constraints and dependencies** (need MAXIMA load case generation, NSTR permanent factor restriction, CTRL BMOD SUPE interaction, EN code references).
4. **Outputs and storage targets** (WinGRAF for shear link stress range; WINGRAF for decompression strains; echo output options for elements and lever arms).

These points are likely intended to be indexed so retrieval can answer questions like: *“What does NSTR SIGT do?”*, *“How is decompression distance chosen?”*, *“Does SIGT affect punching checks?”*, or *“Which parameter activates steel fatigue checks?”*

The table documents input parameters for a fatigue-related stress-range and reinforcement check workflow in a prestressed concrete design program (context given in the surrounding text: items like NSTR, SIGS, SIGT, LC14, CTRL BMOD SUPE, WINGRAF, MAXIMA, etc.). It is structured as a 4-column schema: **Item** (parameter name), **Description** (meaning and rules), **Unit** (typically “–” for non-physical switches/constants), and **Default** (default value if applicable). Most parameters are switches or load/factor identifiers; several are design-layer specific (upper, lower, shear, prestressing steel) and are governed by correction factors for strain/stress reduction in different standards.

Key parameters listed:

- **LS_U, LS_L, LS_V, LS_P**: Define **correction coefficients** \( \lambda_s \) according to standard provisions. The description explicitly references **DIN-FB 102 Appendix A.106.2** or **EN 1992-2** derivations (NN.2.1 / NN.3.1. etc.). Sub-meaning:
  - **LS_U**: *upper reinforcement*
  - **LS_L**: *lower reinforcement*
  - **LS_V**: *shear reinforcement*
  - **LS_P**: *prestressing steel*
  These entries have unit “–” and default “–”, indicating no fixed default is applied (user must provide if needed).

- **LC14**: Controls the **concrete fatigue check** via a product of coefficients described as:  
  \( \lambda c1 \cdot \lambda c2 \cdot \lambda c3 \cdot \lambda c4 \).  
  The program calculates **\( \lambda c0 \)** internally. The description sets a rule:
  - Without LC14 input, the check is based on **EN 1992-1-1 6.8.7 (6.77)** using the stress-range mechanism (example referenced: “with NSTR SIGS 999 …”).
  - With LC14 input, the check is done with **\( \sigma_{c,perm} \)** according to **EN 1992-2 NN.3.2 (NN.112)**.
  Default remains “–” (no inherent value).

- **FACU, FACL, FACV, FACP**: “Increase factors axle load of load model 3”. They scale actions for reinforcement types:
  - **FACU**: upper reinforcement (default **1.0**)
  - **FACL**: lower reinforcement (default **1.0**)
  - **FACV**: shear reinforcement (default **1.0**)
  - **FACP**: prestressing steel (default **1.0**)
  This indicates an optional tuning of load model intensity specifically impacting fatigue/stress-range reinforcement calculations. Units “–”; defaults are numeric.

- **LOCP**: Specifies **local directions of tendons on CTRL LAY 0**. The description clarifies a restriction:
  - Tendons are analyzed exactly in the layer design.
  - Therefore **LOCP is only allowed for CTRL LAY 0**, otherwise it is not permitted.
  It also defines an interpretation by integer setting:
  - **0**: Stress range uses **maximum stress range** across main and transverse reinforcement.
  - **1**: Stress range uses the **stress range of the main reinforcement**.
  - **2**: Stress range uses the **stress range of the transverse reinforcement**.
  Default is “–” (no stated automatic behavior).

Overall, the table serves as a compact specification of inputs that influence: (1) standard-dependent fatigue correction factors for different reinforcement categories, (2) whether/which fatigue model for concrete is activated via **LC14**, and (3) how stress ranges are extracted and which reinforcement category gets driven by the chosen “local tendon direction / stress-range mapping” in **LOCP**, with load-model scaling via **FAC*** defaults of unity.

- **MSTA (Character of the loading)**: Controls the characterization of loading for design calculations. Unit **LIT** with defaults: **YES** (mainly stationary loading) or **NO** (not mainly stationary loading). The “MSTA controls computational reduction of shear stress in shear zone 3 according to DIN1045-1988,” and this table shows that **YES** is the default behavior.

- **AM3**: **Minimum reinforcement of pressed cross sections** given in **percent of the statically required cross section**. Unit is **%**; default is “*” (meaning dependent). The description includes:

  - **SC1**: Concrete material safety bending

The table thus serves as a parameter hub: it links **code-based defaults** (especially DIN1045 variants) with **database-based material classes** and allows controlled overrides of **strengths** and **safety coefficients**, while providing shear-check behavior toggles (**K1S**, **MSTA**) and detailing constraints (**MINC**, **AM3**).

It provides guidance for the governing computation of **shear and/or strength-related stress limits** depending on the selected code framework and combination definition (e.g., “REIN+ULTI”, “REIN”, “ULTI”). The table includes four columns, representing four selectable safety/control sets: **SC1, SC2, SS1, and SS2**.

The surrounding context indicates that:
- The system uses **material database defaults** for concrete and steel (not shown in the table), but safety factors can be adjusted—especially **FC, FY**, and safety multipliers.
- A parameter named **MSTA** controls **reduction of shear stress in shear zone 3** for shear design according to **DIN 1045-1988**.
- The note “**default depending on CTRL REIN/ULTI and the code**” implies these safety factors are selected automatically based on:
  - A control setting (e.g., **CTRL**),
  - whether the design is **REIN** (service/reinforcement-related state) and/or **ULTI** (ultimate limit state),
  - and the chosen code standard.

The table defines geometric parameters for reinforcement placement in a plate/shell context, specifically describing center distances between multiple reinforcement layers and optional limitations of the concrete compression zone. It contains columns **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. All geometric distances are given in **millimetres [mm]**.

### Parameters and meanings

- **H (Plate thickness)**  
  - **Unit:** [mm]  
  - **Default:** `*` (taken as available in the database)  
  - Represents the overall plate (or shell) thickness. In the broader context, these parameters are used to position reinforcement relative to plate edges and to determine concrete cover/compression zone behavior.

- **HA (Centre distance of the upper main reinforcement from the upper plate edge)**  
  - **Unit:** [mm]  
  - **Default:** **35**  
  - Defines where the upper main reinforcement course is located measured by the centre distance from the **upper** surface.

- **DHA (Centre distance of the upper transverse or middle reinforcement from the main reinforcement)**  
  - **Unit:** [mm]  
  - **Default:** **10**  
  - Gives the spacing of the upper transverse (or middle) reinforcement relative to the **upper main** reinforcement. This is essentially an internal layering distance for the upper side.

- **HB (Centre distance of the lower main reinforcement from the lower plate edge)**  
  - **Unit:** [mm]  
  - **Default:** **HA**  
  - Specifies the position of the lower main reinforcement measured from the **lower** edge. By default it mirrors **HA**, implying symmetric cover positioning.

- **DHB (Centre distance of the lower transverse or middle reinforcement from the main reinforcement)**  
  - **Unit:** [mm]  
  - **Default:** **DHA**  
  - Spacing from the **lower main** reinforcement to the lower transverse/middle reinforcement. The default symmetry links it to **DHA**.

- **DDHA (Centre distance of the upper inner reinforcement from the middle reinforcement)**  
  - **Unit:** [mm]  
  - **Default:** **DHA**  
  - Additional inner-layer offset on the upper side, describing a likely three-course reinforcement layout where an “inner” layer exists between main and transverse/middle layers.

- **DDHB (Centre distance of the lower inner reinforcement from the middle reinforcement)**  
  - **Unit:** [mm]  
  - **Default:** **DHB**  
  - Equivalent inner-layer offset on the lower side, defaulting to match **DHB** for symmetry.

- **HPRE (Limitation of the compression zone thickness)**  
  - **Unit:** [mm]  
  - **Default:** `-` (not set)  
  - Used to limit the compression zone thickness for special cases (e.g., hollow plates where design options are enabled through the GEOM/HPRE mechanism). The provided context notes that this enables certain hollow-plate calculations but does **not** trigger a shear design; shear must be checked separately.

### Structural interpretation notes (from surrounding context)

The additional text indicates that some thickness/placement inputs are relevant depending on whether the structure is treated as a **disk** or not. For disks, several values related to reinforcement course definition may have **no effect**. It also states that **GEOM HA, DHA** and **PARA DU, ASU, ASU2** count for one disc side, and the opposite side uses the same reinforcement, meaning the geometry parameters in this table effectively describe one side and are mirrored in output (ASU/ASL placement requirements differ by workflow tool like WINGRAF).

Overall, this table is a compact specification of **layer-to-layer reinforcement spacing and edge cover positions** for upper and lower reinforcement courses, with an optional control (**HPRE**) for compression-zone thickness behavior.

### Table description (RAG-friendly)

This table defines the input parameters for a reinforcement orientation record that controls the **angle of orthogonal/possibly skew steel mesh reinforcement** relative to a **local x-axis** in the structural coordinate system. The record includes four items: **UPP, LOW, X, Y, Z**. It is associated with mesh direction definitions that are referenced by other records such as **DIRE** (orthogonal two-course reinforcement) and **THRE** (skew two- and three-course reinforcement). The angles are measured in **degrees**, and the record remains effective until another **DIRE** or **THRE** record is entered.

#### Angle parameters (UPP and LOW)
- **UPP**: Defines the **angle between the upper main reinforcement direction** and the **local x-axis**.  
  - **Unit:** degrees  
  - **Default:** 0  
  - **Allowed range (as given):** between **0 and 180**  
  - Interpretation: the transverse reinforcement is perpendicular to the main reinforcement in the orthogonal case (handled by DIRE), while the sign convention is consistent with clockwise-positive angle definitions relative to the x-axis.

- **LOW**: Defines the **angle between the lower main reinforcement direction** and the **local x-axis**.  
  - **Unit:** degrees  
  - **Default:** 0  
  - **Allowed range (as given):** between **0 and 180**  
  - Interpretation: sets the orientation for the span (lower) reinforcement main direction; if the system design uses a two-layer mesh concept, this parameter determines its direction relative to the local x-axis.

For disk structures, related surrounding text indicates that certain direction inputs effectively apply to one side and are reused on the other side, and outputs typically require both **ASU** and **ASL** to be placed (with special behavior in “WINGRAF” serving only **ASU**). These details affect how reinforcement placement results are interpreted, though the table itself only specifies parameter meanings.

#### Circular/3D coordinate parameters (X, Y, Z)
These coordinate parameters are used as a **geometric reference definition**, particularly for design cases involving circular plates and for defining orientation direction vectors in **three-dimensional systems**.

- **X**: Centre reference coordinate for **circular plate design**.  
  - **Unit:** meters \([m]_{1001}\)  
  - **Default:** “-” (not specified in the table)

- **Y**: Additional centre reference coordinate for circular plate design and orientation referencing.  
  - **Unit:** meters \([m]_{1001}\)  
  - **Default:** “-” (not specified in the table)

- **Z**: Defines how the design coordinate direction vector is constructed in 3D.  
  - **Unit:** meters \([m]_{1001}\)  
  - **Default:** “-” (not specified in the table)  
  - Meaning (as stated in the table): angles defined with **UPP** and **LOW** refer to the **direction vector** from the input centre toward the **design point**. In the **three-dimensional** case, the axis orientation depends on whether **Z = 0**; additionally, the convention determines which axis is treated as the reference through conditional axis definitions using X and Y when Z is nonzero.

Overall, this table provides: (1) **direction angles** for upper and lower reinforcement main directions relative to the local x-axis, and (2) **reference centre/axis definition inputs** (X, Y, Z) that contextualize the angular directions in circular and/or 3D element situations.

sections: 3.11 GEOM – Input of the Cross Section

content:
The table lists input parameters for **THRE – Definition of Skew 2- and 3-course Reinforcement**, which extends reinforcement modeling by allowing **independent selection of upper (support reinforcement) and lower (span reinforcement) meshes**. In THRE, multiple reinforcement “courses” can be defined (outer/middle/inner). Each input specifies the **directional angle** of a reinforcement course relative to the **local coordinate system’s x-axis**. The angles are measured in **degrees** and are defined as **positive clockwise**. For each course, the angle range is constrained to **0 to 180 degrees**.

Each row contains:
- **Item**: the parameter name (e.g., ABEX, ABMI).
- **Description**: what reinforcement course the angle refers to and the geometric meaning (direction relative to the local x-axis).
- **Unit**: always **degrees**.
- **Default**: the assumed value if not provided (some entries show “-”, meaning no explicit default value is indicated/required).

### Parameters defined in this table
- **ABEX**: angle between the **upper outer reinforcement direction** and the local x-axis. Default **0.0°**.  
- **ABMI**: angle between the **upper middle reinforcement direction** and the local x-axis. Default **90.0°**.  
- **ABIN**: angle between the **upper inner reinforcement direction** and the local x-axis. Default **not specified (“-”)**.

- **BEEX**: angle between the **lower outer reinforcement direction** and the local x-axis. Default **0.0°**.  
- **BEMI**: angle between the **lower middle reinforcement direction** and the local x-axis. Default **90.0°**.  
- **BEIN**: angle between the **lower inner reinforcement direction** and the local x-axis. Default **not specified (“-”)**.

### Practical interpretation
These angles control the orientation of the **main and transverse reinforcement directions** for skew/multi-course layouts. In THRE, the directions for the **upper** and **lower** layers are independent, enabling simultaneous **two- and three-course reinforcement** configurations. The table only covers directional-angle inputs; other THRE concepts (e.g., whether a given course is active and how courses map to the reinforcement layout) are governed by additional records not shown here.

### Modeling linkage (context from surrounding text)
THRE is referenced as being complementary to **GEOM** and **DIRE**: an orthogonal two-course mesh at both sides should typically be specified via **DIRE**, while THRE handles skew layouts. This THRE record remains effective until another **THRE** (or **DIRE**) record is provided.
